stem: pregnant woman is admitted for labor. After continuous pushing, she is now exhausted. The baby is engaged at +2 station and shows minimal variability with late deceleration The mother exhausted and can't push What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: She is in the second stage ("continuous pushing"), the head is engaged at +2 station, and the CTG is non reassuring ("minimal variability with late deceleration"), so the baby needs expedited delivery. When the cervix is fully dilated and the station is +2 or lower, operative vaginal delivery is quicker than CS and is the most appropriate step. Because the mother is exhausted and "can't push", forceps is the preferred instrument (ventouse relies on maternal effort), which matches the related version of this recall keyed to forceps.
why_wrong_block:
A. CS is for a head that is not engaged or is above the ischial spines (for example -3 station, 4/5 palpable), or when instrumental criteria are not met; at +2 in the second stage, instrumental delivery is faster.
C. Reassessing in 1 hour is unsafe with late decelerations and minimal variability; delivery should be expedited now.
D. Oxytocin would increase contractions and worsen fetal hypoxia with late decelerations; it is for inadequate contractions with a reassuring CTG, not an exhausted mother with fetal compromise.
key_concept:
Expedited delivery in second stage: station decides the route.
  • Fully dilated + head engaged at or below the ischial spines (0 station or lower; +2 here) = instrumental (forceps or ventouse)
  • Head above the spines / not engaged (palpable abdominally) = CS
  • Exhausted mother who cannot push = forceps (ventouse needs maternal effort)
  • Late decelerations / minimal variability = do not wait, do not start oxytocin
exam_pearl: Non reassuring CTG at full dilation does not automatically mean CS; if the head is engaged at or below the spines (as at +2), deliver vaginally with instruments.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0268).

stem: 33wk GA, CT type 2 deceleration while she is in labour, +2 station, Severe bleeding And 90/60 hypotensive. What is the management?
why_right: The fetus is distressed (type 2 / late decelerations) and the mother is bleeding and hypotensive (90/60), so delivery must be expedited, and with the head already at +2 station (full dilatation implied) the fastest route is an instrumental vaginal delivery. Because the pregnancy is only 33 weeks, forceps are chosen: the vacuum (ventouse) is generally avoided before 34 weeks because of the risk of fetal intracranial and scalp bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ventouse would be suitable at term with the head at +2 or lower, but it is avoided in preterm fetuses below 34 weeks because of the risk of subgaleal and intracranial hemorrhage.
C. Cesarean section is the route when the cervix is not fully dilated or the head is above +2 station; with the head already at +2 in a fully dilated mother who is bleeding and hypotensive, an instrumental delivery is faster than getting to and through a CS.
key_concept:
Expedite delivery: choose by station, dilatation and gestation.
  • Fully dilated + head at +2 or lower: instrumental delivery
  • Not fully dilated or head above +2: cesarean section
  • Below 34 weeks: forceps, not ventouse
  • Late (type 2) decelerations = uteroplacental insufficiency, needs action
  • Early decelerations = head compression, benign
exam_pearl: Preterm (<34 weeks) and low head flips ventouse to forceps; if the cervix is not fully dilated, the answer becomes CS.

stem: 9-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with pain between her legs after falling from a bicycle. She was screaming from pain in between her legs. She is accompanied by her mother. On examination, with the presence of her mother a bluish hematoma is noted in the left labia. What is the most appropriate management? ( no mention of LARGE)
why_right: This is a vulvar hematoma from a straddle injury (fall from a bicycle) in a child, with a mechanism that fits the injury and no mention of a large or expanding swelling. A non-expanding vulvar hematoma is managed conservatively: ice packs, analgesia and rest, with checks that she can void. Most resolve without intervention.
why_wrong_block:
B. A closed hematoma with intact skin carries no infection indication, so prophylactic antibiotics add nothing.
C. Examination under anesthesia is for a child who cannot be examined adequately, or when there is vaginal bleeding, a suspected penetrating or internal injury, or urethral injury; here the lesion is visible and localized.
D. Surgical evacuation is for an expanding hematoma (any size) or a very large tense one; a non-expanding labial hematoma is treated with ice and observation.
key_concept:
Vulvar hematoma: management depends on expansion.
  • Small or non-expanding: ice, analgesia, observation (or aspiration)
  • Expanding, any size: surgical evacuation and ligation
  • Child: look for urinary retention, vaginal bleeding, penetrating injury
  • Inconsistent history or atypical injury: consider abuse
exam_pearl: Expanding = evacuate, regardless of size; not expanding = ice.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0276).
Compiler note: Large without expanding = Ice. Expanding (regardless to size) = Evacuation.

stem: A 28-week pregnant woman, medically and surgically free, with an uncomplicated pregnancy, complains of shortness of breath with exertion. Physical examination is unremarkable. (I am not sure of the stem but it was about education and prevention)? Another Recall: There Are No Signs Of Heart Failure (Literally Stated In The Stem)
OptA: Reassure her that dyspnea is normal during pregnancy
OptB: Give iron supplements to prevent anemia
why_right: Mild exertional dyspnea is common in normal pregnancy: progesterone increases tidal volume and minute ventilation (physiological hyperventilation), and the enlarging uterus raises the diaphragm. In a medically free woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy, an unremarkable exam and no signs of heart failure, the correct action is education and reassurance that this is physiological.
why_wrong_block:
B. Routine antenatal iron may be part of standard care, but it does not explain or address this complaint: nothing suggests anemia (no pallor, normal exam) and her exertional dyspnea is physiological.
C. Pulmonary function tests are for suspected lung disease (wheeze, cough, abnormal exam, rest dyspnea); with a normal exam they are unnecessary.
key_concept:
Dyspnea in pregnancy: physiological unless red flags.
  • Physiological: gradual, exertional, normal exam and saturation
  • Red flags: dyspnea at rest, orthopnea, tachycardia, chest pain, hemoptysis, hypoxia, abnormal auscultation
  • Red flags point to PE, peripartum cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, asthma
exam_pearl: Any red flag (rest dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxia) turns reassurance into workup.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler short version: 28week pregnant with mild SOB on exertion, exam normal, medically free? A- pulmonary function test, B- reassure as dyspnea is normal in pregnancy (highlighted).

stem: A pregnant woman at 38 weeks of gestation is diagnosed with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Ultrasound assessment shows an amniotic fluid index (AFI) of 3 cm. *Absent end diastolic flow ( came together in same Q )* Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: At 38 weeks, IUGR with absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery and severe oligohydramnios (AFI 3 cm) indicates a compromised fetus, and AEDF at 34 weeks or more is an indication to deliver. A fetus with AEDF has little reserve to tolerate contractions, so delivery is by cesarean section rather than induction.
why_wrong_block:
B. Waiting for spontaneous labor exposes a compromised fetus to the risk of stillbirth; observation suits IUGR with normal Doppler before term.
C. Induction is appropriate for term IUGR with normal umbilical artery Doppler (or isolated oligohydramnios at term); with AEDF the fetus is unlikely to tolerate labor.
D. Reassurance ignores two markers of fetal compromise (AEDF and severe oligohydramnios).
key_concept:
IUGR: umbilical artery Doppler drives timing and mode.
  • Normal Doppler: monitor, deliver at 37 weeks or more (induction acceptable)
  • AEDF: deliver at 34 weeks or more; earlier, daily surveillance
  • REDV: deliver at 32 weeks or more
  • AEDF or REDV: cesarean section preferred
  • Non-reassuring CTG or BPP: deliver
exam_pearl: IUGR at term with normal Doppler = induce; with absent or reversed end-diastolic flow = CS.

stem: Pregnant I think GA is 24 weeks, they found out that the pt didn't receive rubella vaccine, when should the pregnant receive MMR?
why_right: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy because of a theoretical fetal risk. A rubella non-immune pregnant woman is therefore vaccinated postpartum, ideally before discharge; breastfeeding is not a contraindication. This protects her future pregnancies from congenital rubella.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 28 weeks she is still pregnant, and a live vaccine is contraindicated at any gestational age (unlike Tdap, which is given in the third trimester).
C. She is non-immune, so she needs vaccination to protect future pregnancies from congenital rubella syndrome.
D. Live vaccines are not given during pregnancy; if given inadvertently, it is not an indication to terminate, but it is never planned.
key_concept:
Vaccines and pregnancy.
  • Live (MMR, varicella, zoster): before pregnancy or postpartum, never during
  • Influenza (inactivated): any trimester
  • Tdap: each pregnancy, 27 to 36 weeks
  • Avoid conception for about 1 month after MMR
  • Inadvertent rubella vaccination: favorable outcome, no termination
exam_pearl: Non-immune to rubella in pregnancy: avoid exposure now, vaccinate postpartum.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): A pregnant woman did not receive the rubella vaccine prior to pregnancy. When is the appropriate time to administer the rubella vaccine? A. Now B. During the second trimester C. Postpartum. Answer: C (Postpartum).

stem: 27-year-old primigravida presented at 36-weeks of gestation with headache, blurred vision (see lab result). Blood pressure 160/110 mmHg Heart rate 76 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Temperature 36.8 °C Test Result Normal Values Protein ++ absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication for acute treatment of hypertension?
why_right: BP 160/110 with headache, blurred vision and proteinuria at 36 weeks is pre-eclampsia with severe features, and severe hypertension needs urgent IV treatment. The recommended IV agents are labetalol (first line) and hydralazine; since labetalol is not listed, hydralazine is the correct acute choice. Magnesium sulfate is also given for seizure prophylaxis, followed by delivery.
why_wrong_block:
A. Clonidine is not a recommended agent for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy; the acute options are IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or oral nifedipine.
B. Methyldopa is an oral, slow-acting drug for mild or chronic hypertension in pregnancy, not for acute severe hypertension.
D. Sodium nitroprusside is avoided in pregnancy because of fetal cyanide toxicity and is reserved for refractory hypertensive emergencies.
key_concept:
Antihypertensives in pregnancy.
  • Acute severe (≥160/110): IV labetalol first, IV hydralazine second, or oral nifedipine
  • Chronic or mild: oral labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine
  • Severe pre-eclampsia: add magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
  • Avoid: ACE inhibitors and ARBs, nitroprusside
exam_pearl: If labetalol is an option for acute severe BP, pick labetalol; if not, hydralazine. Methyldopa is never the acute drug.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot of another version: primigravid presents w acute headache and blurry vision. labs: bp 152/85, protein +++. What will you give? - hydralazine - methyldopa (no answer marked in screenshot).

stem: A 23-year-old primigravida presented at 32-weeks of gestation with seizures (see lab result). Blood pressure 160/110 mmHg Heart rate 78 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Temperature 36.6 °C Test Result Normal Values Protein +++ absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A first seizure at 32 weeks with severe-range BP (160/110) and protein +++ is eclampsia until proven otherwise. After securing the airway, breathing and circulation, the priority is magnesium sulfate, which stops the current seizure and prevents recurrence (it beats diazepam and phenytoin). Blood pressure control and delivery follow once she is stabilized.
why_wrong_block:
A. Steroids promote fetal lung maturity before a preterm delivery and may be given later, but they do nothing for the seizure; MgSO4 comes first.
B. Diuretics have no role in pre-eclampsia or eclampsia; these women are intravascularly depleted and diuresis worsens placental perfusion. Right only for pulmonary edema.
C. Hydralazine treats severe-range BP and is given alongside, but it neither stops nor prevents seizures. It is right when the question asks for the acute antihypertensive.
key_concept:
Eclampsia sequence: ABC, then MgSO4, then control BP, then deliver.
  • MgSO4 = drug of choice to treat AND prevent eclamptic seizures
  • Acute severe BP (≥160/110): IV labetalol or IV hydralazine (oral nifedipine alternative)
  • MgSO4 toxicity: lost reflexes, respiratory depression; stop drug, give calcium gluconate
  • Steroids <34 weeks for lungs; MgSO4 <32 weeks also gives fetal neuroprotection
exam_pearl: Seizure in pregnancy after 20 weeks: answer MgSO4, not the antihypertensive, unless the lead-in asks specifically about BP.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Pregnant pt, with BP 160/100, headache, then developed seizure. A. oral nifedipine B. hydralazine C. bolus of Mg sulfate (highlighted: C).

stem: old woman, admitted at 35 GA with decreased fetal movement, examination showed fundal height corresponds to 29. Fetal weight is below the 10th centile for the gestational age. Amniotic fluid Index is 3. Umbilical artery end diastolic flow is absent. What's the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: Fetal weight is below the 10th centile
Umbilical artery end diastolic flow is absent
why_right: This is fetal growth restriction (EFW below the 10th centile, fundus 29 at 35 weeks) with severe placental insufficiency: AFI 3 (oligohydramnios), reduced movements and absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery. With absent end-diastolic flow at 34 weeks or more, the fetus should be delivered rather than monitored. A compromised fetus with absent flow and little fluid tolerates contractions poorly, so delivery by cesarean section is preferred over induction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antenatal steroids are taught for deliveries before 34 weeks; at 35 weeks they are not the step that matters and must never delay delivery of a compromised fetus. Right if this were an FGR fetus well before 34 weeks with time to give them.
C. Induction exposes a hypoxic fetus with absent end-diastolic flow and oligohydramnios to hours of contractions, with a high risk of fetal distress. Induction suits FGR with normal or only mildly abnormal Doppler near term.
D. Expectant management (daily Doppler, BPP, NST) is only for absent end-diastolic flow before 34 weeks; at 35 weeks with reduced movements the rule is to deliver.
key_concept:
FGR + umbilical artery Doppler decides timing of delivery.
  • Normal Doppler, reassuring tests: weekly surveillance, deliver at 37 weeks or more
  • Absent end-diastolic flow: deliver at ≥34 weeks; before that daily Doppler, BPP, NST
  • Reversed end-diastolic flow: deliver at ≥32 weeks; before that daily testing
  • Absent or reversed flow at delivery: cesarean favored over induction
  • Decreased movements workup: history, kick count, NST, BPP/US, then Doppler if FGR suspected
exam_pearl: Absent end-diastolic flow is not the time for induction or watchful waiting once past 34 weeks; deliver by cesarean.

stem: A 34-year-old delivered 5 months ago presents with failure to breastfeed her baby, dizziness and fatigue. Her obstetrics history revealed that she had a vaginal delivery complicated with retained placenta and severe postpartum hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A severe postpartum hemorrhage (here from retained placenta) can cause hypovolemic shock and ischemic necrosis of the pituitary, which is enlarged in pregnancy. The earliest sign is failure to breastfeed (prolactin loss), and later anterior pituitary failure gives fatigue and dizziness (ACTH and TSH deficiency). This is Sheehan syndrome, and MRI later shows an empty sella.
why_wrong_block:
A. A pituitary adenoma is unrelated to hemorrhage; a prolactinoma would cause galactorrhea and amenorrhea, not failure of lactation. Right when there is a mass with headache or visual field loss and no obstetric trigger.
C. Lymphocytic hypophysitis is autoimmune pituitary inflammation of late pregnancy or postpartum, usually with headache and mass effect; the history of severe PPH points to ischemic necrosis instead.
D. Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents acutely with a thunderclap headache and altered consciousness, not months later with lactation failure.
key_concept:
Severe PPH + failure of lactation = Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis).
  • Earliest sign: no lactation (low prolactin)
  • Later: secondary amenorrhea, breast atrophy, fatigue, hypotension, hair loss
  • Anterior pituitary affected more than posterior
  • Imaging: empty sella on MRI
  • Treat: replace cortisol first, then thyroxine and sex steroids
exam_pearl: Postpartum woman who cannot breastfeed: look for a history of massive PPH; galactorrhea instead would point to prolactinoma.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is scheduled to undergo a myomectomy due to the presence of a large uterine fibroid. The surgeon is planning to administer medication that will help reduce the size of the uterine fibroid prior to performing the procedure. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to use for this purpose?
highlight_terms_source: reduce the size of the uterine fibroid prior to
why_right: The goal is to reduce the size of a large fibroid before myomectomy. GnRH agonists create a temporary hypoestrogenic state that shrinks fibroids and reduces bleeding, and they also allow anemia to be corrected before surgery. They are used short term (usually a few months) because of menopausal side effects and bone loss.
why_wrong_block:
B. Combined pills can control fibroid bleeding but do not shrink the fibroid; they fit symptom control in a small symptomatic fibroid.
C. An IUD (even a levonorgestrel one) may reduce bleeding but does not shrink the fibroid, and a large fibroid distorting the cavity makes insertion and retention unreliable.
D. Progestogens may reduce bleeding but do not reliably shrink fibroids, and some fibroids grow under progesterone.
key_concept:
Fibroid drug choice depends on the goal.
  • Shrink before surgery: GnRH agonist
  • Control bleeding symptoms: OCP, NSAIDs, tranexamic acid
  • Preop GnRH also stops bleeding so anemia can be corrected
  • GnRH limited to short courses: hot flushes, bone loss
exam_pearl: "Reduce the size" = GnRH; "control the bleeding" = OCP or other medical therapy.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1994).

stem: A 34-year-old woman with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss was seen in the clinic. Which of following is the best predictor for pregnancy complication?
why_right: In a woman with recurrent pregnancy loss, the symptom that best predicts a complication (especially another miscarriage) is vaginal bleeding. It is the most important warning sign in pregnancy at any stage, signalling miscarriage early on and previa or abruption later.
why_wrong_block:
A. Heartburn is a common benign symptom from progesterone relaxing the lower esophageal sphincter; it predicts nothing.
B. Dependent ankle edema is physiological in pregnancy; it matters only with hypertension or proteinuria (pre-eclampsia).
C. Abdominal pain is nonspecific (round ligament pain, GI causes) and a weaker predictor than bleeding; it becomes significant when combined with bleeding (abruption, miscarriage, ectopic).
key_concept:
Vaginal bleeding = the cardinal warning sign of pregnancy complications.
  • First trimester: miscarriage, ectopic, molar pregnancy
  • Painless later bleeding: placenta previa
  • Painful later bleeding: placental abruption
  • Painless bleeding at membrane rupture: vasa previa
exam_pearl: Common benign pregnancy symptoms (heartburn, ankle edema) are distractors; bleeding is the red flag.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents at 18 weeks of gestation with a sudden unexpected rupture of membranes followed by painless expulsion of products of conception. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A loss at "18 weeks" (second trimester) with "sudden unexpected rupture of membranes" followed by "painless expulsion" is the classic picture of cervical incompetence: the cervix dilates silently without contractions, so the membranes prolapse and rupture and the pregnancy is expelled. It typically occurs at about 16 to 24 weeks and is prevented in later pregnancies by cerclage.
why_wrong_block:
A. A bicornuate uterus causes recurrent loss, preterm labor and malpresentation, usually with painful contractions rather than silent painless dilation.
B. A submucous fibroid is linked to early miscarriage, bleeding and pain, not painless mid-trimester membrane rupture.
C. Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) present with hypomenorrhea/amenorrhea, infertility or recurrent early loss after uterine instrumentation.
key_concept:
Cervical incompetence = painless second-trimester cervical dilation with loss or preterm birth.
  • Timing: usually 16 to 24 weeks
  • Clues: painless, sudden ROM, membrane herniation, minimal bleeding
  • Risk factors: prior cone biopsy/LEEP, repeated dilatation, cervical trauma
  • Prevention: cerclage in next pregnancy (around 12 to 14 weeks)
  • First-trimester loss: think chromosomal abnormality instead
exam_pearl: Painless + second trimester = cervix; painful contractions or first trimester point elsewhere.

stem: A 29-year-old primigravida presented at 22 weeks of gestation with mild lower abdominal pain. Abdominal examination reveals that the uterus is corresponding to the gestational age with positive fetal heart. Vaginal examination reveals a short soft cervix, which is 1.5 cm dilated with herniation of fetal membranes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: 1.5 cm dilated with herniation of fetal membranes
why_right: At 22 weeks (second trimester) she has a short soft cervix dilated 1.5 cm with herniating membranes, a viable fetus, a uterus matching dates and only mild pain, with no bleeding or fever. Painless second-trimester cervical dilation is the hallmark of cervical incompetence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Septic abortion needs fever, foul discharge and uterine tenderness, none of which are present.
B. Threatened abortion has bleeding with a closed cervix and is typically first trimester; here the cervix is open and there is no bleeding.
C. Incomplete abortion means bleeding with partial passage of products and an open os; here the fetus is alive in utero and nothing has been expelled.
key_concept:
Cervical incompetence = painless second-trimester cervical dilation.
  • Usually 16 to 24 weeks; membranes may bulge through the os
  • Classic history: painless second-trimester loss or sudden membrane rupture
  • Cervical length <25 mm at 16 to 24 weeks with prior mid-trimester loss: cerclage
  • Threatened = closed os; inevitable = open os, nothing passed; incomplete = open os, partial passage
exam_pearl: Open cervix with bulging membranes but little pain or bleeding in the second trimester: think incompetence, not an abortion category.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot shown under 148 as 'Q:'; answer marked with ** in the screenshot.

stem: A 39-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 20 years was married recently; she and her husband want to get pregnant. The woman has hypertension treated with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic with maintenance of blood pressure at 118/80 mmHg. Her insulin doses are all administered through a continuous insulin infusion pump using insulin aspart. She reported that she would try to become pregnant next month (see lab results). 24 hr urine protein 2000 0.8-14 mg/dl (Male) 2.5-11 mg/dl (Female) Creatinine 88 44-115 mol/L HbA1C 8.0 4.7-5.6 %. What is the best advice at this moment to control her blood sugar and prevent congenital malformation?
OptA: Eliminate snacks and begin to take 3 heavy meals daily
OptB: Substitute an angiotensin receptor blocker for her ACE inhibitor
OptC: Her age and risk factors indicate the need to begin taking a statin at this time
OptD: Delay conception until her HbA1c is as close to normal as possible, if this can be safely achieved
why_right: She plans to conceive next month with an HbA1c of 8.0%. High periconceptional glucose during organogenesis is the main driver of congenital malformations in diabetic pregnancy, so the best advice is to delay conception until HbA1c is as near normal as can be reached safely (generally below 6.5% if this is possible without hypoglycemia).
why_wrong_block:
A. Three heavy meals with no snacks would cause glycemic swings and hypoglycemia on an insulin pump and does nothing to address the high HbA1c.
B. ARBs are as teratogenic as ACE inhibitors; both should be stopped and replaced with a pregnancy-safe drug (labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa). ARB is right only as the switch for ACE-inhibitor cough in a non-pregnant patient.
C. Statins are contraindicated in pregnancy and in women trying to conceive.
key_concept:
Preconception care in pregestational diabetes: optimize glucose first, then conceive.
  • Delay pregnancy until HbA1c is as close to normal as safely possible
  • Stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs and statins before conception
  • Switch to labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa for BP
  • Start high-dose folic acid before conception
  • Assess retinopathy and nephropathy before pregnancy
exam_pearl: Lead-in is about preventing malformations: answer is glycemic control before conception, not a drug swap within the RAAS class.

stem: Which of the following is the common cause of first trimester miscarriage?
why_right: The question asks for the common cause of a first trimester miscarriage. About half of these losses are due to fetal chromosomal abnormalities, most often an autosomal trisomy, which makes it the leading cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Obesity modestly raises miscarriage risk but is a risk factor, not the leading cause.
B. Low folate is linked mainly to neural tube defects, not to most miscarriages.
C. Cervical incompetence causes painless second trimester loss (16 to 24 weeks), not first trimester miscarriage.
key_concept:
Timing of the loss decides the commonest cause.
  • First trimester loss: chromosomal abnormality (mostly trisomy)
  • Second trimester painless loss: cervical incompetence
  • Recurrent loss, treatable cause to screen: antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Risk rises with maternal age, especially after 35
exam_pearl: A past history of cervical incompetence does not change the answer for a current early loss: timing decides.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (screenshot 0362 and typed Q:): 26-year-old 9 weeks pregnant woman with vaginal bleeding then spontaneous abortion; most common cause? A. Trauma B. Infection C. Chromosomal abnormality D. Maternal anatomic anomalies. Answer: C (Chromosomal abnormality).

stem: patient had 3 consecutive miscarriage first trimester week now she pregnant and asking you what is most common cause of abortion
why_right: The key is three consecutive first trimester losses (recurrent miscarriage). Among the listed causes, antiphospholipid syndrome is the most important acquired cause of recurrent early loss: a hypercoagulable state that causes placental thrombosis. It is screened for (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2 glycoprotein I) and treated with low-dose aspirin plus heparin in the next pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cervical incompetence causes painless second trimester losses, not repeated first trimester miscarriages.
C. Uterine anomalies (septum, submucous fibroids, adhesions) can contribute to recurrent loss but are a less common cause than APS in this classic recall. Right when imaging shows a structural lesion such as a septate uterus.
key_concept:
Single early loss vs recurrent loss have different answers.
  • Any single first trimester loss: chromosomal abnormality is commonest
  • Recurrent first trimester loss, treatable cause: APS
  • APS clues: DVT/PE, prolonged APTT, positive lupus anticoagulant, livedo
  • APS in pregnancy: low-dose aspirin + LMWH
  • Recurrent second trimester loss: cervical incompetence
exam_pearl: If chromosomal abnormality is listed, it wins for a single early loss; for recurrent loss with no chromosome option, pick APS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot shown within 151's block; option A highlighted in the screenshot.

stem: A 32-year-old woman 30-week pregnant G1+0+0, presented to the clinic with pruritus and jaundice. There is no fever, abdominal pain, or vomiting. She is not on any Medications and no chronic medical illness (see lab results). Hb 11 120-160 g/L (Female). Platelets count 160 150-400 x 109/L. WBC 7 4.5-10.5 x 109/L. Alkaline phosphatase 700 39-117 IU/L. Alanine aminotransferase 79 5-40 IU/L. Aspartate aminotransferase 100 12-40 IU/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: At 30 weeks she has pruritus and jaundice with a cholestatic pattern (ALP 700, only mild ALT and AST rise) and no fever, abdominal pain or vomiting. Platelets are normal (160) and no hypertension is described. Third-trimester itching with cholestatic liver tests is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; the confirmatory test is raised serum bile acids.
why_wrong_block:
A. Acute viral hepatitis gives malaise, vomiting, RUQ pain and transaminases in the hundreds to thousands, not a mainly ALP-driven itchy picture.
B. HELLP needs hemolysis and low platelets, usually with hypertension and epigastric pain; her platelets are 160 and she has no pain or reported high BP.
C. Budd-Chiari presents with RUQ pain, tender hepatomegaly and ascites in a hypercoagulable patient; she has no pain.
key_concept:
Pregnancy liver disease by trimester and clues.
  • Cholestasis of pregnancy: late 2nd/3rd trimester itch (palms, soles), high bile acids, ALP up; ursodeoxycholic acid; resolves after delivery
  • Fetal risks: stillbirth, meconium, preterm birth, so earlier planned delivery
  • HELLP: hemolysis, raised enzymes, low platelets, hypertension
  • Acute fatty liver: vomiting, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, liver failure
  • Hyperemesis-related LFT rise: first trimester
exam_pearl: Itch without pain or fever in the third trimester = cholestasis; add low platelets or high BP and it becomes HELLP.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot from NCBI (NBK551503): Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (obstetric cholestasis) is a liver disorder in the late second and early third trimester, characterized by pruritus with increased serum bile acids and other LFTs; resolves rapidly after delivery; associated with stillbirth, RDS, meconium passage and fetal asphyxia. Etiology multifactorial: genetic (ABCB4/MDR3 etc.), high estrogen states (multiple pregnancy, OHSS), progesterone sulfated metabolites, low selenium and vitamin D.

stem: Pregnant woman in her 38th week admitted to the labor and delivery ward with 4 cm dilation and "complete breech" presentation. US two days ago showed fetal weight was 2.9kg. CTG is reactive. After 2 hours later there was no change. what to do next?
why_right: She is at term (38 weeks), in labor at 4 cm, with a persistent breech. A non-cephalic presentation at delivery is an indication for cesarean section, and planned vaginal breech birth is reserved for strict criteria with experienced staff. With no progress after 2 hours, the safe next step is cesarean section now, rather than augmenting or waiting.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin augmentation of a breech labor is not appropriate; it pushes a malpresenting fetus toward a risky vaginal breech birth. Oxytocin fits a cephalic active-phase labor with inadequate contractions.
B. Waiting 2 more hours would fit a cephalic labor not yet meeting arrest criteria, but the breech itself is the indication, so delay adds nothing.
D. External cephalic version is offered from about 36 to 37 weeks before labor with intact membranes; once she is in established labor it is not the step to take.
key_concept:
Breech at term: ECV before labor, cesarean once in labor.
  • Not in labor, no contraindication: offer ECV
  • In labor with persistent breech: cesarean section
  • ECV contraindications: labor, previa, non-reassuring CTG, uterine anomaly, multiple pregnancy
  • Cephalic active-phase arrest (≥6 cm, membranes ruptured): no change for ≥4 h with adequate contractions, or ≥6 h with inadequate contractions despite oxytocin = CS
exam_pearl: Do not apply cephalic labor-arrest timing to a breech in labor; the presentation decides the cesarean.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshots: other version '33: A pregnant lady with a completely breech presentation and 5 cm dilated, what to do? A. Reassess B. oxytocin C. c/s D. ECV. Answer: C' (SMLE-GOATs October Survivors, Examiner 5), plus same-stem screenshot. Term + breech + active labor = Cesarean delivery. ACOG/UpToDate: planned CS recommended for most singleton breech fetuses at term; vaginal breech only under strict criteria by experienced providers; if already in labor with persistent breech, proceed with cesarean rather than augmentation.

stem: Pregnant woman in her 38th week admitted to the labor and delivery ward with 4 cm dilation and "breech" presentation. CTG is reactive. After 2 hours later there was no change. What to do next? (Examiner: No type mentioned, just "Breech", weight also not mentioned)
why_right: A term ("38th week") fetus in breech presentation that is already in labor ("4 cm dilation") with no progress is delivered by cesarean section. Persistent non-cephalic presentation at delivery is itself an indication for CS, and planned CS is the recommended route for most term singleton breeches. With no planned vaginal breech delivery, no known breech type and no fetal weight, nothing supports continuing labor, so you proceed to CS rather than augment or wait.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin augmentation is for slow progress with inadequate contractions in a cephalic labor; stimulating a breech labor that is not progressing risks head entrapment and cord problems.
B. Waiting suits a cephalic labor in which the time limits for arrest are not yet reached; here the breech itself is the indication, so waiting only delays the needed CS.
D. ECV is offered before labor (from about 36 to 37 weeks); once she is in established labor with a dilated cervix, version is no longer an appropriate option.
key_concept:
Term breech in labor = cesarean section.
  • Before labor (≥36 to 37 wk, no contraindication): offer ECV
  • ECV fails or declined: planned CS (vaginal breech only in selected cases with skilled staff)
  • Breech already in labor: CS
  • Cephalic, ≥6 cm, adequate contractions, no change for ≥4 h: CS (arrest of dilation)
  • Cephalic, inadequate contractions: oxytocin augmentation
exam_pearl: Do not apply the cephalic labor rules (wait or augment) to a breech; the presentation, not the clock, decides the CS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same as Q158 but the examiner noted no breech type and no weight were mentioned. Term + breech + active labor = Cesarean delivery (ACOG/UpToDate: planned CS recommended for most singleton breech fetuses at term; if already in labor with persistent breech, proceed with cesarean rather than augmentation).

stem: A 37-year-old primigravida with uterine fibroid presented at 34 weeks of gestation with abdominal pain and fever. Examination revealed the cervix is closed, and no uterine contractions are felt. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A pregnant woman with a known fibroid who develops abdominal pain and fever has red (carneous) degeneration, the commonest fibroid complication in pregnancy, caused by rapid growth outstripping its blood supply. The closed cervix and no contractions exclude preterm labor. Red degeneration is self limiting and is managed conservatively: observation with rest, analgesia and hydration.
why_wrong_block:
B. Myomectomy in pregnancy is avoided because of massive hemorrhage and pregnancy loss; red degeneration settles without surgery.
C. There is no obstetric indication to deliver; cesarean would be for fetal distress or another obstetric indication, not for a degenerating fibroid.
D. Delivery does not treat red degeneration and inducing at 34 weeks would add prematurity for no benefit; induction is for indicated delivery such as post-term or term PROM.
key_concept:
Fibroid + pregnancy + acute pain + low grade fever = red degeneration, treat conservatively.
  • Typically second trimester, rapid growth with ischemia
  • Exclude preterm labor and abruption (cervix, contractions, CTG)
  • Rest, analgesia, hydration
  • No myomectomy in pregnancy
exam_pearl: If the cervix were dilating with regular contractions this would be preterm labor, not simple red degeneration.

stem: A postpartum woman who is not breastfeeding comes to the clinic asking when she can start using combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) for contraception. When is it appropriate to start them?
key_concept:
Postpartum COC timing depends on breastfeeding and VTE risk.
  • <21 days postpartum: avoid COCs in everyone (VTE risk)
  • 21 to 42 days, not breastfeeding, no other VTE risk factor: COCs generally acceptable
  • 21 to 42 days with other VTE risk factors: avoid
  • ≥42 days (6 weeks): no postpartum restriction
  • Breastfeeding: avoid estrogen early (suppresses milk); prefer progestogen-only methods
exam_pearl: Two questions decide it: breastfeeding? extra VTE risk factors? Under 21 days COCs are never right, and 9 or 12 weeks are not real cut-offs.

stem: When to give dose of antibiotic preoperatively in a pregnant woman with PPROM. She was going to OR for CS?
why_right: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis for cesarean delivery is a single dose given within 60 minutes before skin incision, so tissue levels peak when the skin is cut. PPROM does not change this timing; for a CS in labor or after membrane rupture, an adjunct (azithromycin) is often added to cefazolin.
why_wrong_block:
A. A dose at 30 minutes still falls inside the window, but the rule examined is "within 60 minutes before incision"; 30 minutes is not the defining time point.
C. 90 minutes is outside the 60 minute window for the usual cefazolin dose, so tissue levels may already be falling at incision.
D. A 120 minute window applies only to drugs needing long infusions (vancomycin, fluoroquinolones), not to the standard beta-lactam given for CS.
key_concept:
Prophylaxis = single dose timed to the incision.
  • Cesarean: first-generation cephalosporin within 60 min before skin incision (not after cord clamping)
  • Vancomycin or fluoroquinolone: start within 120 min
  • Redose for long surgery or heavy blood loss
  • Prolonged postoperative courses add resistance, not protection
exam_pearl: Older teaching gave CS antibiotics after cord clamping; current practice is before incision.

stem: A case of a 45 year-old female patient of 35 weeks gestational age. Scheduled for C/S. Taking her pregnancy vitamins. Her BMI is 31. No risk of VTE mentioned. What should be her VTE prophylaxis?
OptB: Continue her vitamins and no prophylaxis needed
key_concept:
Post-CS VTE prophylaxis is risk based.
  • All CS: early mobilisation, hydration, mechanical compression
  • CS + extra risk factors (age >35, BMI ≥30, multiple pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, immobility): add LMWH
  • Prior VTE or thrombophilia: LMWH
  • LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy; warfarin is avoided
  • Aspirin in pregnancy = pre-eclampsia prevention, not VTE
exam_pearl: Count risk factors: CS alone = mobilisation and mechanical measures; CS plus extra factors = add LMWH; aspirin is never the VTE prophylaxis answer.
compiler_note:
⚠ Image audit: The compiler marked this answer tentatively ('??' / 'not sure' / needs re-correction) — see the compiler note.
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0419).
Compiler note: Not sure BUT management principle: for women undergoing cesarean delivery, all get early mobilization; add pharmacologic prophylaxis (LMWH) if additional risk factors (e.g., BMI >=30). BMI 31 = additional VTE risk factor, so she qualifies for mechanical + pharmacologic prophylaxis (enoxaparin). B (no prophylaxis) incorrect.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with a BMI of 48 kg/m² presents to the infertility clinic. Both she and her husband have normal fertility investigations. They been married for one year. She has been counseled on weight loss before. What is the best health promotion and illness prevention advice for her?
why_right: A BMI of 48 (class III obesity, above the BMI ≥40 threshold) in a woman who has already been "counseled on weight loss before" meets criteria for bariatric surgery, which gives the largest and most durable weight loss. Since both partners' fertility work-up is normal, her obesity is the modifiable factor, and surgery is the most effective health promotion step for both fertility and long-term health.
why_wrong_block:
B. Semaglutide is an option for weight loss, but it is less effective than surgery at BMI 48 and must be stopped before conception because GLP-1 agonists are not used in pregnancy.
C. Lifestyle change and calorie restriction are the first step for anyone with obesity, but she has already been counseled; at BMI 48 after failed lifestyle advice, escalation is needed.
D. Observation ignores a severe modifiable risk factor for infertility, pregnancy complications and chronic disease.
key_concept:
Weight management ladder by BMI and response.
  • All: lifestyle (diet, exercise, behaviour) first
  • Failed lifestyle, BMI ≥30 (or ≥27 with comorbidity): add drug therapy
  • BMI ≥40, or ≥35 with comorbidities, after failed nonsurgical measures: bariatric surgery
  • After bariatric surgery: defer pregnancy for at least 12 months (often 12 to 24) during rapid weight loss
exam_pearl: "Already counseled" means lifestyle has failed; with BMI ≥40 that points to surgery, not more advice.

stem: A 36-year-old woman who is hypertensive on hydrochlorothiazide and losartan presents to the clinic because of the absence of her menstrual cycle for 2 months. She is asymptomatic. Her physical examination is unremarkable. A pregnancy test was done and was positive (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment adjustment?
highlight_terms_source: pregnancy test was done and was positive
why_right: A hypertensive woman on "losartan" now has a "positive" pregnancy test. ARBs (and ACE inhibitors) are fetotoxic, mainly causing fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios, so losartan must be stopped and replaced with a pregnancy-safe agent. Methyldopa is a classic safe choice, so the right "treatment adjustment" is to discontinue losartan and start methyldopa.
why_wrong_block:
A. Continuing losartan exposes the fetus to ARB-induced renal toxicity; it is never acceptable once pregnancy is confirmed.
B. Chronic hypertension still needs control in pregnancy; the fix is switching to a safe drug, not stopping all treatment.
D. Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor, which carries the same fetal renal toxicity as an ARB, so this swap does not solve the problem.
key_concept:
Pregnancy: stop ACE inhibitors and ARBs; switch to a pregnancy-safe antihypertensive.
  • Safe oral: labetalol (first line), methyldopa, nifedipine
  • Safe IV (severe): labetalol, hydralazine
  • Avoid: ACE inhibitors, ARBs (fetal renal toxicity)
  • Best timing: switch at preconception counselling
exam_pearl: Enalapril and losartan look like different classes but both block the RAAS; any option keeping an ACEi or ARB is wrong in pregnancy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): woman with hypertension on losartan had secondary amenorrhea and discovered she is pregnant; current BP 140/90; what should she do? A- Stop losartan, B- continue losartan, C- stop losartan and start methyldopa (highlighted).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room complaining that her period has not stopped for the past 15 days. Now she is feeling drowsy and easily fatigued and sometimes faints. Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
highlight_terms_source: period has not stopped for the past 15 days
drowsy and easily fatigued and sometimes faints
why_right: Bleeding for "15 days" with "drowsy", "easily fatigued" and "faints" points to symptomatic anaemia from heavy uterine bleeding. The first step is to quantify blood loss with a CBC (haemoglobin guides the need for transfusion and urgency) and to exclude a pregnancy-related cause with beta-hCG, because a 45-year-old is still of reproductive age. These results decide the next management (resuscitation, hormonal therapy or D&C).
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound is part of the later workup for structural causes (fibroids, polyps, endometrial thickness), but it does not assess anaemia or pregnancy first in a fainting patient.
B. A urine pregnancy test alone excludes pregnancy but ignores the symptomatic anaemia; the CBC is the urgent part here.
C. D&C is reserved for severe or refractory bleeding after assessment; it is not done before knowing haemoglobin and pregnancy status.
key_concept:
Heavy bleeding with anaemia symptoms: CBC + beta-hCG first, then treat by severity.
  • Always exclude pregnancy in reproductive-age AUB
  • CBC assesses anaemia and need for transfusion
  • Acute AUB options: IV estrogen, COCP or oral progestogen, tranexamic acid
  • D&C for severe or refractory bleeding
  • Over 45: endometrial sampling to exclude hyperplasia/cancer
exam_pearl: If the stem gives a low haemoglobin already, the next step becomes transfusion rather than more tests.

stem: A 22-year-old patient presented to the Emergency Department with history of expulsion of products of conception at home. On examination, cervix were closed with minimal vaginal bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: "Expulsion of products of conception at home" (tissue passed) plus a closed cervix with only minimal bleeding is a complete abortion: the uterus has emptied itself and the os has closed. Ultrasound would show an empty uterus, and she is managed conservatively with outpatient follow-up.
why_wrong_block:
B. Inevitable abortion has an OPEN cervix with products still inside (not yet passed); here tissue has passed and the os is closed.
C. Threatened abortion has a closed cervix but NO tissue passed and a viable fetus on ultrasound; she has already expelled the pregnancy.
D. Incomplete abortion has an OPEN cervix with only partial passage of tissue and usually heavier bleeding; a closed os with minimal bleeding argues against retained products.
key_concept:
Classify miscarriage by cervix (open/closed) x tissue (passed/not passed).
  • Closed + not passed + viable fetus: threatened
  • Closed + not passed + nonviable: missed
  • Closed + passed: complete
  • Open + not passed: inevitable
  • Open + partially passed: incomplete
  • Fever, foul discharge, uterine tenderness: septic
exam_pearl: The os splits open cases: no tissue passed = inevitable; tissue passed or protruding through the os = incomplete. Tissue passed with a CLOSED os = complete.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Highlighted option annotated 'MG'.

stem: A 33-year-old 7 weeks' pregnant woman presented with vaginal bleeding and a history of passing tissue at home. Examination revealed an open cervix with moderate vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound: Intrauterine 3x4 cm tissue seen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: history of passing tissue at home
why_right: Passed tissue, an open cervix and 3x4 cm retained intrauterine tissue mean incomplete abortion, and the bleeding is moderate. Moderate to heavy bleeding or instability is the indication for surgical evacuation of the uterus (suction evacuation or D&C), which removes the source of bleeding definitively.
why_wrong_block:
A. Expectant management suits a stable patient with light bleeding; moderate bleeding with a sizeable retained mass calls for active evacuation.
B. Oxytocin works poorly on the first trimester uterus and does not remove retained products.
C. Methergine may contract the uterus and reduce bleeding, but it does not empty the retained tissue, which is the definitive treatment.
key_concept:
Incomplete, inevitable or missed abortion: choose by bleeding and stability.
  • Stable, light bleeding: expectant (first trimester) or medical (misoprostol)
  • Moderate to severe bleeding or unstable: resuscitate + surgical evacuation
  • Complete abortion: reassure, outpatient follow up
  • Threatened abortion: conservative
exam_pearl: The word 'moderate' (or heavy) bleeding with retained tissue pushes the answer to evacuation, not observation.

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman presented with abdominal cramps and mild vaginal bleeding. Examination revealed an open cervix with mild bleeding. Ultrasound: A 7-week viable intrauterine pregnancy. Which of the following is the most likely type of abortion she had?
why_right: Cramps and bleeding with an open cervix, no tissue passed, and a still viable 7-week intrauterine pregnancy is inevitable abortion. Once the os has opened the pregnancy cannot be saved, even though fetal activity may still be seen on ultrasound.
why_wrong_block:
A. Missed abortion has a closed os and a nonviable fetus; here the os is open and the fetus is viable.
C. Incomplete abortion requires partial passage of tissue; nothing has been passed here.
D. Threatened abortion also has a viable fetus, but the os is closed; an open os moves it to inevitable.
key_concept:
Classify early pregnancy bleeding by the os first, then tissue passage, then viability.
  • Closed os + viable IUP = threatened
  • Closed os + nonviable fetus, nothing passed = missed
  • Open os + nothing passed = inevitable
  • Open os + partial passage, tissue retained = incomplete
  • Closed os + everything passed, empty uterus = complete
  • Fever, foul discharge, uterine tenderness = septic
exam_pearl: A heartbeat does not make it threatened: the open os overrides viability and makes it inevitable.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1044H).

stem: A 36-year-old woman is evaluated during her first prenatal visit for medical history of hypothyroidism, for which she has taken levothyroxine 125 µg/d, for the last 2 years. On physical examination, no goiter or cervical lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular, pulmonary and abdominal examinations are unremarkable (see lab results). BP 100/73, HR 87, RR 13, Temp 36.5 °C, SpO2 97%, BMI 23. TSH 4.4 (0.4-5.0), Free T4 9.5 (8.5-15.2 pmol/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment of this patient's hypothyroidism now?
highlight_terms_source: history of hypothyroidism, for which she has taken levothyroxine 125
why_right: At her first prenatal visit, a woman on levothyroxine needs a dose increase: thyroxine requirement rises early in pregnancy, and the TSH target is tighter (about 0.5 to 2.5 in the first trimester). Her "TSH 4.4" is inside the general range but above the pregnancy target, and her free T4 is low-normal, so increasing the dose protects fetal neurodevelopment. Recheck TSH about every 4 weeks in the first half of pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Continuing the same dose is right in a non-pregnant patient with TSH within range; in pregnancy, TSH 4.4 is above target and demand will keep rising.
C. Decreasing is right only for over-replacement (suppressed TSH, high free T4); here TSH is high for pregnancy.
D. Stopping levothyroxine would cause maternal and fetal hypothyroidism; known hypothyroidism needs lifelong replacement, more so in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Hypothyroid + pregnant = increase levothyroxine as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.
  • Typical increase about 20 to 30% (e.g. two extra doses per week)
  • TSH target in pregnancy about 0.5 to 2.5 (first trimester)
  • Check TSH about every 4 weeks until mid-pregnancy
  • Non-pregnant: recheck TSH 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change
  • Return to pre-pregnancy dose after delivery
exam_pearl: A "normal" TSH by the lab range can still be too high for pregnancy.

stem: Gravida 10 weeks with a past history of painless delivery at 18 weeks and loss the baby. What to follow in this pregnancy?
highlight_terms_source: painless delivery at 18 weeks and loss the baby
why_right: "Painless delivery at 18 weeks" is a second-trimester loss from painless cervical dilation, the classic history of cervical incompetence. With that history, prophylactic (history-indicated) cerclage is placed at 12 to 14 weeks, after the first-trimester miscarriage window and once a viable pregnancy and normal early scan are confirmed. At 10 weeks now, she is planned for cerclage at 13 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance is right after an ordinary sporadic first-trimester miscarriage; a painless mid-trimester loss carries a high recurrence risk and needs intervention.
C. 15 weeks is later than the usual 12 to 14 week window for history-indicated cerclage; she is seen at 10 weeks, so it can be booked in the ideal window, and waiting only adds the risk that the cervix starts to open.
D. Serial cervical length ultrasound is right when the history does not clearly fit cervical incompetence (unspecified loss, or prior preterm birth); with a classic painless second-trimester loss, the plan is planned cerclage.
key_concept:
Cervical incompetence: manage by history and gestational age.
  • Prior painless 2nd-trimester loss, seen early: history-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 wk
  • Prior spontaneous preterm birth or nonspecific loss: serial TVUS cervical length 16 to 24 wk; cerclage if <25 mm
  • No such history, short cervix (<25 mm) on scan: vaginal progesterone
  • Cerclage generally not placed after 24 wk
exam_pearl: "Painless" plus "second trimester" is what earns early cerclage; a vague prior miscarriage gets scans instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Previous painless delivery at 18 weeks suggests cervical incompetence. A prior second-trimester painless loss is an indication for history-indicated (prophylactic) cerclage, performed at 12–14 weeks, most commonly 13 weeks. 1 painless 2nd-trimester loss: prophylactic cerclage 12–14 wks; short cervix incidentally (<25 mm) without history: vaginal progesterone; short cervix + prior preterm birth: cerclage. Confirmed q (screenshot): Preg woman 10 wks GA, previous midtrimester painless cervical dilatation and loss of preg: cerclage at 13 wks (history indicated) / cerclage 18 wks / US. If she meets the classical ACOG definition, answer is A (Hx indicated cerclage); if not, answer is US to measure cervical length.

stem: Female came with a history previous miscarriage in her first pregnancy, now came for counseling about the second pregnancy (she is in 10 weeks).
OptD: Serial ultrasound to assess cervical length and dilation
why_right: The stem gives only "previous miscarriage" with no timing and no painless cervical dilation, so a diagnosis of cervical incompetence cannot be made and history-indicated cerclage is not justified. The safe plan is surveillance: serial transvaginal ultrasound of cervical length, intervening only if the cervix shortens. This recall is the twin of the version that adds "painless mid-trimester loss", where the answer switches to cerclage at 13 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cerclage at 13 weeks is history-indicated only after a painless second-trimester loss typical of cervical incompetence; one unspecified miscarriage does not meet that bar.
B. Placing a cerclage at a fixed 18 weeks without a scan finding is neither history-indicated (12 to 14 wk) nor ultrasound-indicated (cervix <25 mm), so it has no indication.
C. Digital assessment of cervical dilation is subjective and detects change late; transvaginal cervical length is the objective, earlier predictor.
key_concept:
Which history earns which plan.
  • Painless 2nd-trimester loss: cerclage at 12 to 14 wk
  • Unclear or nonspecific prior loss / risk: serial transvaginal cervical length (16 to 24 wk)
  • Cervix <25 mm with prior 2nd-trimester loss: cerclage before 24 wk
  • Ordinary first-trimester miscarriage: usually chromosomal, low recurrence, routine care
exam_pearl: Read the history word by word: "painless" and "mid-trimester" flip the answer from scans to cerclage.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Exam trick: Painless 2nd trimester loss: cerclage at 12–14 weeks. Just one previous miscarriage (unspecified): serial cervical length monitoring.

stem: Female pregnancy 10 weeks GA came with a history of (one mid trimester abortion at 18 weeks happened by painlessly dilatation of the cervix and spontaneous expulsion) of fetus in her first pregnancy, now came for counseling about the second pregnancy.
OptD: Serial ultrasound to assess cervical length and dilation
highlight_terms_source: one mid trimester abortion at 18 weeks happened by painlessly dilatation of the cervix and spontaneous expulsion
why_right: "One mid trimester abortion at 18 weeks" by "painless dilatation of the cervix and spontaneous expulsion" is the textbook history of cervical incompetence. Such a history is the indication for prophylactic (history-indicated) cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks, so at 10 weeks she is counselled for cerclage at 13 weeks, after the first-trimester miscarriage risk has passed and an early scan has confirmed a normal viable pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
B. 18 weeks is the gestation at which she lost the last pregnancy; waiting until then risks the cervix already dilating, and history-indicated cerclage belongs at 12 to 14 weeks.
C. Digital checks for dilation are subjective and detect cervical change too late; they do not replace a planned cerclage in a woman with this history.
D. Serial cervical length scans (16 to 24 wk, cerclage if <25 mm) are right when the history is not diagnostic, e.g. an unspecified loss or a prior spontaneous preterm birth; with a classic painless mid-trimester loss, cerclage is planned.
key_concept:
Cervical incompetence = painless 2nd-trimester dilation and loss.
  • Classic history, early booking: history-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 wk
  • Prior spontaneous preterm birth or nonspecific loss: serial TVUS cervical length 16 to 24 wk; cerclage if <25 mm
  • Nonspecific prior miscarriage: serial cervical length surveillance
  • No history, short cervix <25 mm: vaginal progesterone
  • No cerclage after 24 wk
exam_pearl: Same options as the "previous miscarriage only" twin; the word "painless" makes this one cerclage at 13 weeks.

stem: Female came with a history of cervical incompetence in her first pregnancy, now came for counseling about the second pregnancy.
OptD: Serial ultrasound to assess cervical length and dilation
highlight_terms_source: history of cervical incompetence in her first pregnancy
why_right: The stem gives an established diagnosis of cervical incompetence in the first pregnancy and she is now being counselled for the next one. A known incompetent cervix is managed by gestational age: before 24 weeks the answer is a prophylactic (history indicated) cerclage, placed electively early in the second trimester at about 13 to 14 weeks. Waiting until this point lets the first trimester miscarriage risk pass and allows viability and early anomaly screening to be confirmed.
why_wrong_block:
B. 18 weeks is too late for an elective history indicated stitch; by then the cervix may already be shortening or dilating. A cerclage in this window is usually ultrasound indicated (short cervix) or rescue (dilated cervix), not planned prophylaxis.
C. Repeated digital assessment of dilation is crude and detects change only once it is advanced; it does not prevent loss in a woman already known to have an incompetent cervix.
D. Serial transvaginal cervical length scans between 16 and 24 weeks are the strategy for a woman with a single prior loss or preterm birth whose diagnosis is uncertain (cerclage if length <25 mm). Here the diagnosis is already stated, so the planned stitch is chosen.
key_concept:
Cervical incompetence: timing of cerclage decides the answer.
  • Known diagnosis, early pregnancy: history indicated cerclage at 13 to 14 weeks
  • Seen at 8 weeks: wait, do not stitch the same week
  • Prior loss, uncertain diagnosis: serial TVUS cervical length from 16 to 24 weeks
  • Cervical length <25 mm before 24 weeks: ultrasound indicated cerclage
  • Cerclage is generally not offered after 24 weeks
  • Hegar dilator testing is for the non-pregnant state only
exam_pearl: "Known cervical incompetence" plus early pregnancy = cerclage at 13 to 14 weeks; "previous preterm birth" without a diagnosis = cervical length surveillance.

stem: 43 years old female came with heavy vaginal bleeding and she want contraceptive methods. Which test to do is compulsory before advising any treatment?
key_concept:
AUB work-up: decide between imaging and endometrial sampling.
  • Always: pregnancy test and CBC
  • Structural cause suspected or first imaging: TVUS
  • Age ≥45 with AUB: endometrial biopsy
  • Age <45: biopsy if unopposed estrogen (obesity, PCOS) or AUB persists despite medical treatment
  • Postmenopausal bleeding: biopsy if endometrium >4 to 5 mm on TVUS
  • CT has no role in AUB evaluation
exam_pearl: Read for duration and age: a long history of AUB or age ≥45 turns the answer from ultrasound to endometrial biopsy.
