stem: 18 years old female came with painful cycle and acne on face, pain disturbs her routine and she is already on NSAIDs which are not helpful anymore. What's next?
highlight_terms_source: painful cycle and acne on face
already on NSAIDs which are not helpful
why_right: An 18 year old with painful periods that "disturb her routine" has primary dysmenorrhea, and she is already on NSAIDs which are not helpful anymore. When NSAIDs fail, the next step is hormonal therapy with combined oral contraceptive pills, which suppress ovulation and reduce endometrial prostaglandin production. The acne is a bonus clue: the combined pill raises SHBG and lowers free androgens, so it treats both problems at once.
why_wrong_block:
B. Progestin only pills are not the standard step after NSAID failure and, being progestin dominant without estrogen, they do not improve acne and may worsen it. They are chosen when estrogen is contraindicated (for example migraine with aura, high VTE risk).
C. Continuing NSAIDs is the answer only for a patient not yet tried on them or with partial response; here the stem states they no longer help, so the ladder must move up.
key_concept:
Primary dysmenorrhea ladder.
  • Step 1: lifestyle (heat, exercise)
  • Step 2: NSAIDs, first line drug
  • Step 3: combined OCP when NSAIDs fail
  • Acne or hirsutism plus dysmenorrhea: COCP doubly useful
  • Failure of hormones or onset after 25 years: think secondary cause (endometriosis), consider laparoscopy
exam_pearl: First presentation of dysmenorrhea = NSAIDs; "NSAIDs not helpful anymore" = OCP.

stem: Gravida 39 and obese and baby good weight. What to do to avoid shoulder dystocia?
why_right: A term (39 weeks) obese woman with a large baby is at risk of shoulder dystocia. The deck's other version of this recall keys suprapubic pressure: together with McRoberts positioning it is the first line, simple external manoeuvre that adducts and dislodges the impacted anterior shoulder, so it is the one to have ready at delivery. Strictly, no manoeuvre prevents dystocia; the question is asking which listed manoeuvre is used first.
why_wrong_block:
B. Gaskin (all fours) manoeuvre is an alternative used after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail, mainly in a mobile woman without an epidural; it is not the first step.
C. Rubin manoeuvre is an internal rotational manoeuvre (pressure on the back of the anterior shoulder) used as a second line step once external manoeuvres have failed.
key_concept:
Shoulder dystocia sequence (HELPERR style).
  • Call for help, stop maternal pushing, no fundal pressure
  • First line: McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure
  • Second line: internal manoeuvres (Rubin, Woods screw) or delivery of the posterior arm
  • Then: all fours (Gaskin)
  • Last resort: Zavanelli, symphysiotomy
  • True prevention: planned caesarean for suspected marked macrosomia, especially with diabetes
exam_pearl: Fundal pressure worsens impaction; suprapubic pressure, not fundal, is the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version: Pregnant woman with diabetes mellitus and obesity evaluated for obstetric risk; most appropriate maneuver to help prevent shoulder dystocia during delivery? A. Rubin B. Suprapubic pressure C. Gaskin D. Zavanelli. Answer B (check) = suprapubic pressure.

stem: Gravida came with chances of DVT. What do you give?
why_right: For a pregnant woman at risk of (or with) DVT, low molecular weight heparin is the anticoagulant of choice. It does not cross the placenta, has a predictable dose response, needs little monitoring, and carries less bleeding, heparin induced thrombocytopenia and osteoporosis risk than unfractionated heparin. The same answer applies to the related recall of PE in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block: A. Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes warfarin embryopathy in the first trimester and fetal bleeding later, so it is avoided in pregnancy. It is acceptable postpartum (safe with breastfeeding) and is a special exception in some women with mechanical heart valves.
key_concept:
Anticoagulation in pregnancy.
  • Prophylaxis or treatment of DVT or PE: LMWH (enoxaparin)
  • Severe renal impairment or need for rapid reversal: unfractionated heparin
  • Warfarin: avoid antenatally; fine postpartum and in breastfeeding
  • DOACs: avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding
  • Massive PE with instability: thrombolysis still considered
exam_pearl: Pregnant + clot = LMWH; warfarin only after delivery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related 'Q:': Pregnant lady with PE: A. LMWH (highlighted) B. Warfarin C. Thrombolytic D. (wasn't clear if stable or not).

stem: Abruptio placenta risk factor?
why_right: Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally sited placenta, and its most common risk factor is maternal hypertension (chronic hypertension and pre-eclampsia), followed by smoking and abdominal trauma. Hypertensive vascular damage in the decidual arteries leads to retroplacental bleeding and separation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diabetes is linked to macrosomia, polyhydramnios, pre-eclampsia and stillbirth, but it is not a classic direct risk factor for abruption.
C. A fibroid lying behind the placenta is a recognised but uncommon association with abruption; it is far less frequent than hypertension, so it is not the answer to a "risk factor" or "most common" question.
key_concept:
Abruption risk factors: hypertension first.
  • Most common: maternal hypertension or pre-eclampsia
  • Smoking and cocaine use
  • Abdominal trauma
  • Previous abruption
  • Sudden uterine decompression (PROM with polyhydramnios, delivery of first twin)
  • Advanced maternal age, multiparity
exam_pearl: Previa = previous CS and multiple gestation; abruption = hypertension, smoking, trauma.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version: What is the most common risk factor for abruptio placenta? A. Folate deficiency B. Short umbilical cord C. Maternal hypertension (highlighted) D. Premature rupture of membrane.

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman with 7 weeks' amenorrhea presented to the clinic with a history of passing tissue at home and vaginal bleeding. Examination revealed mild vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix. Which of the following is the most likely abortion type?
highlight_terms_source: mild vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix
why_right: She passed tissue at home and now has only mild bleeding with a closed cervix. Tissue passed plus a closed os means the uterus has emptied itself: complete abortion. Ultrasound would be expected to show an empty uterus, and she can be followed up as an outpatient.
why_wrong_block:
B. Inevitable abortion has an open os with no tissue passed yet; here the os is closed and tissue has already come out.
C. Threatened abortion has a closed os but no tissue passage and a viable ongoing pregnancy; passing tissue rules it out.
D. Incomplete abortion has tissue passed but the os stays open because products are still retained; a closed os means the uterus is empty.
key_concept:
Classify early pregnancy bleeding by the os first, then tissue passage, then viability.
  • Closed os + viable IUP = threatened
  • Closed os + nonviable fetus, nothing passed = missed
  • Open os + nothing passed = inevitable
  • Open os + partial passage, tissue retained = incomplete
  • Closed os + everything passed, empty uterus = complete
  • Fever, foul discharge, uterine tenderness = septic
exam_pearl: Passed tissue does not automatically mean incomplete: the os decides. Closed os = complete, open os = incomplete.

stem: A 81 year old woman with pelvic organ prolapse complains of chronic constipation she reports that she needs to press inside the vagina with her hand to facilitate stool evacuation she is currently unfit for surgery what is the most appropriate management until she becomes fit for surgery?
highlight_terms_source: needs to press inside the vagina with her hand to facilitate stool evacuation
why_right: An 81 year old with pelvic organ prolapse who must press inside the vagina to evacuate stool (vaginal digitation, the hallmark of a posterior compartment rectocele) is unfit for surgery. Elderly or comorbid women who cannot have repair are managed conservatively, and the vaginal pessary mechanically supports the prolapse and relieves the obstructed defaecation while she waits to become fit for posterior colporrhaphy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laxatives soften stool and can be an adjunct, but they do not correct the anatomical pocket that traps stool, so she would still need to digitate.
C. Pelvic floor exercises suit mild prolapse or stress incontinence in motivated, usually younger women; in an 81 year old with symptomatic prolapse they will not give timely mechanical relief.
D. Systemic HRT does not treat prolapse. Local vaginal estrogen may be added to protect atrophic mucosa when a pessary is fitted, but it is an adjunct, not the management.
key_concept:
Pelvic organ prolapse: patient fitness decides.
  • Elderly, comorbid or unfit for surgery: pessary (conservative)
  • Mild or asymptomatic prolapse: pelvic floor exercises
  • Young, healthy, symptomatic: surgery
  • Rectocele (constipation, digitation): posterior colporrhaphy
  • Cystocele (urinary symptoms): anterior colporrhaphy
  • Vault or uterine descent: sacrospinous fixation
exam_pearl: "Unfit for surgery" in any prolapse stem points to the pessary.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same question shown twice. Numbered 240 (p73) is a stub: 'An 80 year old complaining of urinary incontinence and inability to defecate unless using her finger to help. Unfit for surgery.' with only 'A. Vaginal pessary' (highlighted). The fuller unnumbered 'Q:' version (printed on p74 after 241's options) is used here; it also highlights Vaginal pessary.

stem: An 80-year-old woman known case of prosthetic heart valve on warfarin and bedridden. Diagnosed as stage 3 pelvic organ prolapse. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Every clue rules out surgery: age 80, "bedridden", and a prosthetic heart valve "on warfarin" (surgery would need anticoagulation bridging with high bleeding and thrombotic risk). A patient who is not a surgical candidate is managed conservatively, and the conservative treatment of choice for even advanced (stage 3) prolapse is a vaginal pessary, which needs no anesthesia.
why_wrong_block:
B. Sacrocolpopexy is an abdominal or laparoscopic operation under general anesthesia. It is a good choice for apical or vault prolapse in a fit, sexually active woman, not in this frail anticoagulated patient.
C. Le Fort colpocleisis is the least invasive surgical option for frail women who are not sexually active, but it is still surgery. It is considered when a pessary fails or cannot be retained; pessary comes first here.
D. Vaginal hysterectomy with repair is a standard surgical option for uterine prolapse in a fit patient, but this elderly, bedridden, anticoagulated woman is not a surgical candidate.
key_concept:
Prolapse management is driven first by fitness for surgery, then by wish to keep sexual function.
  • Elderly, comorbid, non-surgical candidate: pessary
  • Fit woman, uterine prolapse: vaginal hysterectomy with repair
  • Vault prolapse after hysterectomy: sacrospinous fixation or sacrocolpopexy
  • Frail, not sexually active, pessary fails: colpocleisis
exam_pearl: Warfarin, a prosthetic valve and bedridden status are clues that point away from any operation.

stem: Patient with hypertension, with heavy bleeding and anemia, what contraceptive she can use?
why_right: She needs contraception that also treats heavy bleeding and anaemia while being safe with hypertension. The levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena) is progestin only, so it carries no estrogen related rise in blood pressure or clot risk, and it markedly reduces menstrual blood loss, allowing the anaemia to recover. It is also a first line treatment for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding in its own right.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tubal ligation is permanent and does nothing for the heavy bleeding or anaemia; it suits a woman who has completed her family and has no menstrual problem.
C. Condoms are safe in hypertension but have no effect on bleeding and are less effective with typical use.
D. Combined OCPs do reduce bleeding, but the estrogen raises blood pressure and VTE risk, so they are avoided in a hypertensive woman; they are chosen for heavy bleeding in a normotensive woman without estrogen contraindications.
key_concept:
Contraception with heavy menstrual bleeding.
  • No contraindication to estrogen: LNG IUD or COCP
  • Hypertension, smoker over 35, migraine with aura, VTE history: avoid estrogen
  • Estrogen contraindicated plus heavy bleeding: LNG IUD (Mirena)
  • Cardiac patient on anticoagulants: progestin only method
  • Copper IUD: may worsen heavy bleeding
exam_pearl: Copper IUD increases bleeding; the hormonal Mirena reduces it, do not confuse them.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Need a method that reduces bleeding and contains no estrogen (estrogen may raise BP and clot risk). Mirena (levonorgestrel IUD): progestin only; reduces heavy menstrual bleeding up to 80-90%; improves anemia; safe in hypertension. Hypertension + heavy menstrual bleeding = choose a progestin-only method, especially the levonorgestrel IUD.

stem: 24 yo primigravida, on 14 wks US was showing molar pregnancy, suctioning dilation was done and pt is now reassessing Bhcg level weekly, pt was advised to use contraceptive: What is the best method (were asking what give more health benefits)
why_right: After suction evacuation of a molar pregnancy she is on weekly beta-hCG surveillance, and a new pregnancy must be avoided because its hCG would hide persistent trophoblastic disease. The combined OCP is reliable, does not interfere with hCG measurement, and regulates cycles so abnormal bleeding stands out; it also adds the health benefits the stem asks about (lighter regular periods, lower ovarian and endometrial cancer risk).
why_wrong_block:
A. The vaginal ring is also a combined hormonal method and would be acceptable, but it offers no advantage over the pill here and the pill is the standard recommended method during hCG follow-up.
C. An IUD is avoided until hCG has normalised because, if persistent disease invades the uterus, there is a risk of perforation and the device can cause irregular bleeding that confuses follow-up.
D. Tubal ligation is permanent and inappropriate in a 24 year old primigravida who will want future pregnancy once surveillance is complete.
key_concept:
Molar pregnancy follow-up.
  • Treatment: suction evacuation, then serial beta-hCG
  • Weekly hCG until undetectable for 3 weeks, then monthly
  • Reliable contraception throughout surveillance
  • Preferred: combined OCP (does not affect hCG)
  • Avoid IUD until hCG is normal
  • Rising or plateauing hCG: persistent GTN, needs chemotherapy work-up
exam_pearl: Post-mole contraception = OCP; no IUD while hCG is still detectable.

stem: woman became pregnant soon after delivery. She Had 4 Months Of Amenorrhea After Delivery. What Is the Best Way To Properly Date Her Pregnancy?
why_right: She conceived during 4 months of postpartum amenorrhoea, so she has no reliable LMP to count from. When the LMP is unknown or unreliable, the most accurate way to date a pregnancy is an early first trimester ultrasound measuring crown-rump length, which reflects gestational age before individual growth differences appear.
why_wrong_block:
A. Naegele's rule needs a known, reliable LMP with regular cycles; she has had no period since delivery, so there is no LMP to use.
C. Second trimester biometry (head and femur measurements) is used only if a first trimester scan was missed; it is less accurate because biological variation in fetal size grows with gestation.
D. Third trimester ultrasound is the least accurate for dating since fetal size varies widely by then; it assesses growth and wellbeing, not gestational age.
key_concept:
Dating a pregnancy.
  • Known regular LMP: Naegele's rule (day +7, month +9)
  • Unknown or unreliable LMP (breastfeeding, postpartum amenorrhoea, irregular cycles, recent pill): first trimester TVUS
  • Up to 13+6 weeks: crown-rump length
  • Later: head circumference and femur length
  • Accuracy falls with each trimester
  • Abdominal circumference: growth and fetal weight, not dating
exam_pearl: Amenorrhoea before conception = no usable LMP, so date by early CRL, not by dates.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recall: P2 woman with positive pregnancy test, delivered 4 months ago, fully breastfeeding, amenorrhea since delivery. How to date pregnancy? Highlighted: First trimester ultrasound.

stem: Pregnant woman in her 38th week presented with 4 cm dilation and breech presentation. 2 hours later there was no change. CTG is reactive. (everything generally fine)
highlight_terms_source: 2 hours later there was no change
why_right: A persistent breech presentation in established labor ("38th week", "4 cm") is itself an indication for cesarean section, and here labor has also failed to progress ("2 hours later no change"). In breech labor, slow progress is treated as a warning of possible disproportion, so the safe answer is delivery by emergency CS rather than waiting or augmenting. The reactive CTG only means there is no fetal distress; it does not make vaginal breech delivery the preferred route.
why_wrong_block:
A. Waiting is the cephalic rule (active phase arrest needs about 4 hours of adequate contractions without change). With a breech in labor and no progress, delaying only adds risk without changing the need for CS.
C. ECV is offered before labor (from about 36 to 37 weeks) to turn a breech; once she is in established labor at 4 cm it is no longer the appropriate step.
D. She is already in labor, so there is nothing to induce; using oxytocin to push a non progressing breech labor is avoided because poor progress may signal disproportion.
key_concept:
Breech at term: before labor = offer ECV; in labor = CS (especially with poor progress).
  • ECV timing: before labor, about 36 to 37 weeks onward
  • ECV contraindications: multiple pregnancy, placenta praevia, non reassuring CTG, uterine malformation, IUGR, significant third trimester bleeding
  • CS indications: fetal distress, obstructed labor, active phase arrest, non cephalic presentation at delivery
  • Cephalic active phase arrest: 4 h adequate contractions no change = CS; inadequate contractions = oxytocin first
exam_pearl: Do not apply the cephalic "wait 4 hours / give oxytocin" ladder to a breech in labor; breech plus no progress = CS.

stem: 34 weeks gestation, came with 6 hrs ruptured membrane, no contraction, -1 sation, no fever and vitally stable, and her fundal height is 30 weeks, speculum exam revealed meconium stained liquor, best next step?
OptC: Prophylactic Abx and induction of labor
OptD: Prophylactic Abx and wait for 37 weeks
why_right: This is PPROM at 34 weeks ("6 hrs ruptured membrane", "no contraction", before 37 weeks). The decisive extra clue is "meconium stained liquor" (with a fundal height lagging at 30 weeks), which argues against prolonging the pregnancy, so delivery is chosen; with no fetal distress or obstetric contraindication, the route is induction of labor. Antibiotic prophylaxis is added because she is preterm with ruptured membranes and unknown GBS cover, which is why C is preferred over induction alone.
why_wrong_block:
A. Induction is the right delivery plan but incomplete: a preterm woman with ruptured membranes going into labor should also receive antibiotic (GBS) prophylaxis.
B. Immediate CS needs fetal distress or an obstetric indication (for example malpresentation or a non reassuring CTG); meconium alone with a stable mother does not mandate CS.
D. Expectant management towards 37 weeks is only an option at 34 weeks or more when mother and fetus are reassuring; meconium stained liquor and a small fundal height remove that option here.
key_concept:
PPROM management depends on gestational age and on whether there is a reason to deliver.
  • PROM = rupture before labor at ≥37 weeks; PPROM = before 37 weeks
  • Confirm rupture: sterile speculum, ferning, nitrazine
  • <34 weeks, stable: expectant care with steroids and latency antibiotics
  • ≥34 weeks: delivery (or expectant care only if fully reassuring), with GBS prophylaxis
  • Chorioamnionitis, fetal compromise, meconium: deliver; route by usual obstetric indications
exam_pearl: Meconium in PPROM is a reason not to wait, but it is not by itself an indication for CS; induce plus antibiotics.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Answer line: A or C. Meconium-stained fluid suggests possible fetal stress, supporting not delaying delivery. CS not required without fetal distress or obstetric indication; no contraindication to vaginal birth, so induction. Best answer: C. A (induction only) incomplete, GBS prophylaxis should be given. B not indicated. D contraindicated in PPROM >=34 weeks.
Other marked answers: Answer line: A or C

stem: 30-year-old woman with a history of infertility for 6 years complains of severe dysmenorrhea unrelieved by naproxen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The combination of infertility for 6 years and severe dysmenorrhea unrelieved by naproxen (NSAID failure) in a woman of 30 is the classic picture of endometriosis. Ectopic endometrial implants cause cyclic inflammatory pain and adhesions that distort tubal and ovarian anatomy, explaining the infertility. Primary dysmenorrhea usually responds to NSAIDs, so failure points to a secondary cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Endometritis presents with fever, uterine tenderness and offensive discharge, typically after delivery, miscarriage or instrumentation; it is not a cause of long-standing cyclic pain.
B. Leiomyomata typically cause heavy menstrual bleeding and an enlarged irregular uterus; they can affect fertility, but severe NSAID-resistant dysmenorrhea with infertility is the endometriosis pattern.
D. Pelvic congestion syndrome causes chronic dull pelvic pain worse on prolonged standing, usually in multiparous women with pelvic varices; it is not linked to infertility.
key_concept:
Endometriosis = 3 Ds + infertility.
  • Dysmenorrhea (secondary, NSAID resistant), dyspareunia (deep), dyschezia
  • Exam: fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodularity, adnexal mass (endometrioma)
  • Most common site: ovary
  • Diagnosis: laparoscopy (visual plus histology)
  • Adenomyosis: older multiparous, menorrhagia, diffusely enlarged tender uterus
exam_pearl: Severe dysmenorrhea + infertility = endometriosis; add menorrhagia and a boggy enlarged uterus in a multiparous woman and it becomes adenomyosis.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0113).

stem: Most common subtype HPV in cervical cancer?
why_right: HPV 16 and 18 are the high-risk oncogenic types and together cause the large majority (about 70%) of cervical cancers worldwide. HPV 16 is the single most common type, mainly in squamous cell carcinoma, while HPV 18 is relatively more frequent in adenocarcinoma. Their E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate p53 and Rb, driving dysplasia.
why_wrong_block:
A. The pair given (11/12) is not a cervical cancer pair; HPV 6 and 11 are the low-risk types causing genital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, and HPV 12 is not a genital type.
C. HPV 31 and 33 are high-risk types that can cause cancer, but they are far less common than 16 and 18; 32 and 36 are not recognised cervical cancer types.
D. HPV 44 is a low-risk type associated with benign genital lesions; it is not a significant cause of cervical cancer.
key_concept:
HPV types: high risk = cancer, low risk = warts.
  • 16: most common overall, squamous cell carcinoma
  • 18: relatively more adenocarcinoma
  • 16 + 18 together: about 70% of cervical cancers
  • 6 and 11: genital warts, laryngeal papillomas (low risk)
  • Other high risk: 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 (covered by the 9-valent vaccine)
  • Oncogenesis: E6 degrades p53, E7 inactivates Rb
exam_pearl: Warts = 6/11; cancer = 16/18. Do not mix the two pairs.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0109).

stem: 22-year-old woman with a history of multiple sexually transmitted diseases presented at the 37th gestational week for her first antenatal visit. The obstetrician is concerned about this maternal infection which may cause conjunctivitis and blindness in the newborn. Which of the following is the most suitable for health promotion and illness prevention?
highlight_terms_source: conjunctivitis and blindness in the newborn
why_right: Maternal genital infections that cause neonatal conjunctivitis and blindness are Chlamydia and gonorrhea, acquired during vaginal birth. She has a history of multiple STIs and is at 37 weeks with no antenatal care, so prevention means treating the mother before delivery. Azithromycin is the pregnancy-safe treatment for Chlamydia (gonorrhea is covered by adding ceftriaxone), which removes the source before the baby passes through the birth canal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance ignores a high-risk woman with a transmissible infection; it fits only a low-risk patient with negative screening.
C. Screening the newborn after delivery is too late to prevent exposure; neonatal eye prophylaxis and treatment are added on, but the preventive step is treating the mother first.
D. Referral delays treatment at 37 weeks when delivery is imminent; uncomplicated Chlamydia or gonorrhea is treated directly by the obstetrician.
key_concept:
Ophthalmia neonatorum: prevent by treating the mother before delivery.
  • Gonococcal: early (first days), purulent, can perforate cornea and cause blindness; ceftriaxone
  • Chlamydial: later (about 1 to 2 weeks), most common; azithromycin in pregnancy
  • Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy
  • Newborn: routine eye prophylaxis; treat Chlamydia conjunctivitis with oral erythromycin
exam_pearl: Health promotion/prevention wording points to treating the mother now, not screening or treating the newborn later.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0436).

stem: A pregnant woman is admitted for labor. After continuous pushing, she is now exhausted. The baby is engaged at +2 station and shows minimal variability with late deceleration The mother exhausted and can't push What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: She is in the second stage ("continuous pushing"), the head is engaged at +2 station, and the CTG is non reassuring ("minimal variability with late deceleration"), so the baby needs expedited delivery. When the cervix is fully dilated and the station is +2 or lower, operative vaginal delivery is quicker than CS and is the most appropriate step. Because the mother is exhausted and "can't push", forceps is the preferred instrument (ventouse relies on maternal effort), which matches the related version of this recall keyed to forceps.
why_wrong_block:
A. CS is for a head that is not engaged or is above the ischial spines (for example -3 station, 4/5 palpable), or when instrumental criteria are not met; at +2 in the second stage, instrumental delivery is faster.
C. Reassessing in 1 hour is unsafe with late decelerations and minimal variability; delivery should be expedited now.
D. Oxytocin would increase contractions and worsen fetal hypoxia with late decelerations; it is for inadequate contractions with a reassuring CTG, not an exhausted mother with fetal compromise.
key_concept:
Expedited delivery in second stage: station decides the route.
  • Fully dilated + head engaged at or below the ischial spines (0 station or lower; +2 here) = instrumental (forceps or ventouse)
  • Head above the spines / not engaged (palpable abdominally) = CS
  • Exhausted mother who cannot push = forceps (ventouse needs maternal effort)
  • Late decelerations / minimal variability = do not wait, do not start oxytocin
exam_pearl: Non reassuring CTG at full dilation does not automatically mean CS; if the head is engaged at or below the spines (as at +2), deliver vaginally with instruments.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0116).
Compiler note: Screenshot version: 37 week GA, +2 station, vertex palpable in vagina, CTG minimal variability with late decelerations, mother exhausted and can't push. Options: A- Forceps, B- Ventous, C- C/S, D- Fetal Blood Sampling. Athar: A (Probably Confirmed). Choice of instrumental delivery: Exhausted/can't push = Forceps (regardless of GA).
Other marked answers: Athar screenshot: A. Forceps

stem: Female with 6 weeks amenorrhea, bhcg was 700, they gave a table with range of bhcg for weeks 0-4, 0-6 and 0-7. Her bhcg was in normal range according to the table they gave, but TVUS showed no intrauterine pregnancy, what will you do?
why_right: A positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine pregnancy on TVUS is a pregnancy of unknown location. Her bhCG of 700 is normal for dates but below the discriminatory zone, so an empty uterus is expected and not diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy. The next step is to repeat bhCG in 48 hours: a viable intrauterine pregnancy rises appropriately (classically about doubling), while an ectopic or failing pregnancy rises slowly, plateaus or falls.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methotrexate is given only once an ectopic pregnancy is established; giving it now could terminate a normal early intrauterine pregnancy.
C. With bhCG below the discriminatory zone, a repeat scan in 48 hours is unlikely to show a sac; repeat TVUS once bhCG passes about 1500 to 2000.
key_concept:
Pregnancy of unknown location: follow the bhCG trend, then rescan.
  • Step 1: repeat bhCG in 48 hours
  • Viable IUP: appropriate rise over 48 hours (classically about doubling; current minimum about 35% to 53%)
  • Ectopic or failing pregnancy: slow rise, plateau or fall
  • Discriminatory zone about 1500 to 2000: above it, an empty uterus on TVUS strongly suggests ectopic
exam_pearl: Empty uterus with bhCG below the discriminatory zone is not ectopic yet; repeat bhCG, do not treat.

stem: A 9-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with pain between her legs after falling from a bicycle. She was screaming from pain in between her legs. She is accompanied by her mother. On examination, with the presence of her mother a bluish hematoma is noted in the left labia. What is the most appropriate management? (no mention of LARGE)
why_right: This is a vulvar hematoma from a straddle injury (fall from a bicycle) in a child, with a mechanism that fits the injury and no mention of a large or expanding swelling. A non-expanding vulvar hematoma is managed conservatively: ice packs, analgesia and rest, with checks that she can void. Most resolve without intervention.
why_wrong_block:
B. A closed hematoma with intact skin carries no infection indication, so prophylactic antibiotics add nothing.
C. Examination under anesthesia is for a child who cannot be examined adequately, or when there is vaginal bleeding, a suspected penetrating or internal injury, or urethral injury; here the lesion is visible and localized.
D. Surgical evacuation is for an expanding hematoma (any size) or a very large tense one; a non-expanding labial hematoma is treated with ice and observation.
key_concept:
Vulvar hematoma: management depends on expansion.
  • Small or non-expanding: ice, analgesia, observation (or aspiration)
  • Expanding, any size: surgical evacuation and ligation
  • Child: look for urinary retention, vaginal bleeding, penetrating injury
  • Inconsistent history or atypical injury: consider abuse
exam_pearl: Expanding = evacuate, regardless of size; not expanding = ice.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0118).
Compiler note: Typed 'Answer: A'. Fuller 'Q:' version: severe pain, screaming in the ER, hematoma bluish and tender; options A. Ice Bag placement (highlighted), B. Prophylactic antibiotics, C. Examination under anesthesia, D. Surgical evacuation of hematoma.

stem: A 59-year-old postmenopausal woman with a history of breast cancer on tamoxifen presents with 2 months of abnormal vaginal bleeding. An endometrial biopsy was attempted but inadequate. What is the next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: endometrial biopsy was attempted but inadequate
why_right: Postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen must be investigated for endometrial cancer, because tamoxifen stimulates the postmenopausal endometrium (polyps, hyperplasia, carcinoma). The office biopsy was "inadequate", so cancer has not been excluded; the next step is hysteroscopy with directed biopsy, which visualises the cavity and samples or removes focal lesions such as polyps that blind sampling misses.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stopping tamoxifen does not diagnose the cause of bleeding and the decision belongs to her oncology plan; malignancy must be excluded first.
C. Hysterectomy is too radical without a tissue diagnosis; it becomes appropriate once histology shows cancer or atypical hyperplasia.
key_concept:
Postmenopausal bleeding: tissue diagnosis first, escalate sampling if inconclusive.
  • PMB with endometrial thickness >4 mm on TVUS (or persistent bleeding): endometrial biopsy
  • On tamoxifen, TVUS thickness is unreliable (subendometrial changes), so tissue sampling is preferred
  • Inadequate or nondiagnostic biopsy, or persistent bleeding: hysteroscopy with directed biopsy
  • Tamoxifen: raises risk of polyps, hyperplasia and endometrial cancer
  • Symptomatic polyp: hysteroscopic polypectomy
exam_pearl: An inadequate biopsy is never reassurance; in PMB it means hysteroscopy, not observation or surgery.

stem: Case of ectopic pregnancy received methotrexate; her bHCG were: on day 1 (3000), on day 4 (3100) on day 7 (2900). What to do next?
why_right: After single dose methotrexate, the response is judged by comparing day 4 with day 7, not day 1. Here bhCG went from 3100 on day 4 to 2900 on day 7, a fall of only about 6.5%, which is less than the required 15%. An inadequate fall (plateau or <15%) in a stable patient means a second dose of methotrexate should be considered, with the day 4 and day 7 checks repeated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simply continuing follow up is only for a fall of more than 15% between day 4 and day 7; this response is inadequate.
B. Surgery is for rising bhCG, hemodynamic instability or signs of rupture, or failure after repeat dosing; her level is not rising and she is stable.
C. An inadequate response to single dose treatment is managed with a second single dose, not by switching to a multi dose regimen.
key_concept:
Methotrexate follow up: compare day 4 with day 7.
  • Fall >15%: weekly bhCG until undetectable
  • Plateau or fall <15%: consider second methotrexate dose
  • Rising bhCG: surgical management
  • Day 1 to day 4 rise is expected and is not failure
  • Instability or severe pain: laparoscopy
exam_pearl: The rise from day 1 to day 4 is a trap; only the day 4 to day 7 change counts.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot: 'Right answer is D', confirmed by UpToDate.

stem: This picture came in exam with fishy smell secretion and picture of clue cells and Whiff’s test positive. What diagnosis?
why_right: A fishy smelling discharge, a positive whiff test (amine odor with KOH) and clue cells on the wet mount are the classic triad of bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella with loss of lactobacilli, pH above 4.5). Clue cells, epithelial cells studded with bacteria, are the single most specific microscopy finding. Treatment is metronidazole for the patient only.
why_wrong_block:
A. Candidiasis gives itching with thick, curdy, odorless discharge, pseudohyphae on KOH, normal pH and a negative whiff test.
B. Trichomoniasis gives frothy yellow green discharge with strawberry cervix and motile flagellated protozoa on wet mount, not clue cells; partners must be treated.
key_concept:
Vaginitis is decided by microscopy.
  • BV: gray/milky fishy discharge, pH >4.5, whiff positive, clue cells; metronidazole, partner not treated
  • Trichomonas: frothy yellow green, strawberry cervix, flagellated protozoa; metronidazole plus partner
  • Candida: cottage cheese, odorless, pseudohyphae, normal pH; topical azoles
exam_pearl: Trichomoniasis can also smell and have a high pH; the clue cells are what make it BV.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Arabic note in source: the same picture exactly (wet mount showing clue cells).

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Room with sudden severe abdominal pain for the last three hours, sharp and radiating to the right shoulder. She has an irregular menstrual cycle, and the last episode was six weeks ago (see report). Pelvic ultrasound: Abundant fluid collected in the pouch of Douglas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: last episode was six weeks ago
Abundant fluid collected in the pouch of Douglas
why_right: A woman of reproductive age with a missed period ("last episode six weeks ago") and "sudden severe" abdominal pain is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. Pain "radiating to the right shoulder" is referred diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum, and "abundant fluid in the pouch of Douglas" is blood: this is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Septic miscarriage: presents with fever, offensive discharge and uterine tenderness after a miscarriage or instrumentation, not sudden pain with shoulder tip radiation.
B. Appendicular mass: develops over days after appendicitis, with right iliac fossa mass and fever; it does not cause sudden pain with a large haemoperitoneum.
C. Incomplete miscarriage: vaginal bleeding with cramping and passed tissue through an open os; it does not fill the pouch of Douglas with fluid.
key_concept:
Amenorrhea + acute abdominal pain + free fluid = ruptured ectopic.
  • Shoulder tip pain = blood irritating the diaphragm
  • Guarding, rigidity = peritonism from haemoperitoneum
  • Unruptured: unilateral pain, spotting, adnexal mass, empty uterus
exam_pearl: Irregular cycles do not exclude pregnancy; any woman of reproductive age with acute pain needs pregnancy excluded first.

stem: A 34-year-old multiparous woman presents to the Maternal Health Clinic at 28 weeks' gestation with coughing and difficulty in breathing. She appears restless and uncomfortable. Auscultation of the lung fields shows bilateral rhonchi. The nail beds and oral mucous membranes appear pale. She is allergic to dust, pollen, mold, and animal hair. There is no history of smoking. She reports that the symptoms began 2 days prior and started with coughing up clear-colored phlegm. Blood pressure is 124/72 mmHg, heart rate is 120/min, respiratory rate is 24/min. Which of the following tests is initially most appropriate?
highlight_terms_source: allergic to dust, pollen, mold, and animal hair
why_right: The picture is asthma in pregnancy: atopy ("allergic to dust, pollen, mold, and animal hair"), cough with clear phlegm, dyspnea, bilateral rhonchi, and no smoking history. The lead in asks for the test that is initially most appropriate, and spirometry confirms airflow obstruction (and its reversibility) and grades severity; it is safe in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Chest X-ray is for suspected pneumonia or a complication (fever, purulent sputum, focal signs); it does not diagnose asthma.
C. ABG assesses a severe exacerbation with suspected respiratory failure; it is not the first diagnostic test for suspected asthma.
D. The pale nail beds suggest anemia, but anemia does not explain rhonchi and atopy; hemoglobin does not evaluate the respiratory complaint.
key_concept:
Atopic patient with cough, dyspnea and wheeze/rhonchi = asthma: spirometry first.
  • Spirometry: obstructive pattern with reversibility after bronchodilator
  • CXR: only if pneumonia or complication suspected
  • ABG: severe or life threatening attack
  • Spirometry and asthma treatment are safe in pregnancy
exam_pearl: The pale mucosa is a distractor toward hemoglobin; the atopy plus rhonchi drive the answer.

stem: A 15-week pregnant woman who smokes regularly is concerned about the risk of ADHD or other problems in her baby due to smoking. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Refer her to a smoking cessation program
why_right: She is a pregnant smoker who is already worried about harm to her baby, which makes this a good moment to act. In pregnancy the first line intervention is referral to a smoking cessation (stop smoking) service for structured behavioral support, because the safety and benefit of drug therapy in pregnancy are less certain than outside pregnancy. Her concern should also be addressed by explaining the real fetal risks (growth restriction, low birth weight, preterm birth).
why_wrong_block:
A. NRT is first line outside pregnancy; in pregnancy it can be added with behavioral support if counselling alone does not work, but it is not the first step.
C. Bupropion is not recommended in pregnancy and is not a first line approach here (it is also contraindicated in seizure disorders).
D. Non nicotine chewing gum is not a smoking cessation treatment: it gives no nicotine and no behavioral support, so it does nothing for dependence or her risk to the baby.
key_concept:
Smoking cessation in pregnancy: behavioral support first.
  • Pregnant smoker: refer to stop smoking service
  • If counselling alone fails: NRT may be added with support
  • Bupropion and varenicline: avoided in pregnancy
  • Non pregnant adult: NRT first line, varenicline second line
  • Main fetal effect of smoking: growth restriction / low birth weight
exam_pearl: "Pregnant" flips the general rule: NRT is first line in non pregnant adults, but referral to cessation support comes first in pregnancy.

stem: A woman presents with dyspepsia, weight loss, and shortness of breath. Examination shows a 12 cm irregular adnexal mass and an enlarged uterus. Diagnosis?
why_right: A 12 cm irregular adnexal mass is the dominant finding, and irregular contour and large size favour malignancy. Vague GI symptoms ("dyspepsia"), weight loss and shortness of breath (suggesting ascites or a malignant pleural effusion) are the typical late presentation of ovarian cancer, which often spreads through the peritoneum before causing pelvic symptoms. The enlarged uterus does not change the primary diagnosis; it may reflect mass effect, a coexisting condition, or estrogen from a functioning ovarian tumor.
why_wrong_block:
A. Uterine sarcoma presents as a rapidly enlarging uterus, often with postmenopausal bleeding, and arises in the uterus rather than as a large irregular adnexal mass.
C. Endometrial cancer typically presents with postmenopausal bleeding and a bulky uterus; there is no bleeding here, and the adnexal mass is the main lesion.
D. Cervical cancer presents with postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding and a visible cervical lesion, not an adnexal mass with GI symptoms.
key_concept:
Adnexal mass features favouring malignancy:
  • Postmenopausal age, family history of ovarian, breast or colon cancer
  • Solid or complex, irregular, fixed, bilateral
  • Ascites, rapid growth
  • Irregular multilocular solid tumor >10 cm (IOTA malignant feature)
  • Vague symptoms: bloating, dyspepsia, early satiety, weight loss
exam_pearl: Vague GI symptoms plus weight loss plus a large irregular adnexal mass = ovarian cancer until proven otherwise; do not let the enlarged uterus pull you to a uterine diagnosis.

stem: A woman who is 30 weeks pregnant is being asked about the most critical vaccine to give at this stage of pregnancy?
why_right: At 30 weeks the vaccine that matters most is the pertussis-containing one, given at 27 to 36 weeks so maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn before its own primary series starts. Pertussis is most lethal in the first months of life, which is why this dose is given in every pregnancy. The keyed option (DTaP) stands for this pertussis booster; the adult formulation actually used in pregnancy is Tdap.
why_wrong_block:
A. Varicella is live attenuated and contraindicated in pregnancy; a non-immune woman is vaccinated before conception or postpartum.
B. MMR is live attenuated and contraindicated in pregnancy; rubella non-immune women receive it postpartum.
D. Live attenuated vaccines as a class (MMR, varicella, live zoster, smallpox) are avoided in pregnancy because of theoretical fetal risk.
key_concept:
Pregnancy vaccines: inactivated yes, live no.
  • Tdap: every pregnancy, 27 to 36 weeks (neonatal pertussis protection)
  • Inactivated influenza: any gestational age in season
  • Hepatitis B, meningococcal: not live, can be given if indicated
  • HPV: not live but deferred until after pregnancy
  • MMR, varicella, live zoster: contraindicated; give preconception or postpartum
exam_pearl: "Most critical at 30 weeks" = pertussis booster; if the stem says "any trimester, flu season" the answer becomes influenza.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Printed label '308- 309' covers this single screenshot.

stem: Baby delivered dead (Stillbirth case). Which of the following is best to use for chromosomal analysis?
why_right: The baby is already delivered dead, so prenatal sampling is no longer possible and fetal tissues degrade quickly after death, often failing to grow in culture. Placental tissue (a sample from the fetal side, near the cord insertion) stays viable longer than fetal tissue and reflects the fetal karyotype, so it gives the best yield. Chromosomal microarray on this tissue is useful because it does not need living cells.
why_wrong_block:
A. Umbilical cord sampling as cordocentesis is a prenatal procedure on a living fetus; after delivery a cord segment can be sent, but placental tissue gives the higher culture yield.
B. Amniocentesis before delivery is an excellent sample when fetal death is diagnosed in utero, but after delivery amniotic fluid is no longer available.
C. Cord blood from a stillborn has clotted, non-viable cells that usually fail to culture; it is the best source only in a live birth.
key_concept:
Stillbirth genetic testing: choose the sample with the most viable cells.
  • Fetus still in utero: amniocentesis gives the highest culture yield
  • After delivery: placental tissue near the cord insertion is preferred
  • Other options: segment of umbilical cord, internal fetal tissue (e.g. costochondral junction)
  • Microarray works on non-viable tissue, unlike conventional karyotype
exam_pearl: If the stem says fetal death diagnosed BEFORE delivery, the answer flips to amniocentesis.

stem: Pregnant woman presents with mild shortness of breath on exertion. Physical examination is normal and she has no past medical history. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Reassure the patient that dyspnea is normal in pregnancy
highlight_terms_source: mild shortness of breath on exertion
why_right: Physiological dyspnea affects most pregnant women: progesterone drives hyperventilation and the woman perceives the increased minute ventilation as breathlessness. Here the dyspnea is mild, on exertion only, the examination is normal and there is no past history, so the correct management is reassurance.
why_wrong_block: A. Pulmonary function tests add nothing when the history and exam are benign; they are for suspected asthma or other lung disease (wheeze, cough, abnormal exam).
key_concept:
Physiological dyspnea of pregnancy vs red flags.
  • Physiological: gradual, exertional, normal exam, normal saturation, no chest pain
  • Red flags: sudden onset, dyspnea at rest, tachycardia, hypoxia, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, leg swelling
  • Suspected PE: leg Doppler first, then V/Q scan or CTPA
  • Orthopnea, edema, late pregnancy or postpartum: think peripartum cardiomyopathy, get echo
exam_pearl: Any abnormal vital sign or sudden onset turns "reassure" into a PE workup.

stem: 34 Year Old Female came to the clinic for recurrent pregnancy loss. What is the best predictive symptom?
why_right: In a woman with recurrent pregnancy loss, the symptom that best predicts a complicated pregnancy, especially another loss, is vaginal bleeding. It is the key warning sign of miscarriage, abruption and previa, and it should prompt urgent assessment with ultrasound.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal pain is common and nonspecific in pregnancy (round ligament, GI causes); it is a weaker predictor than bleeding.
C. Heartburn is a benign, common symptom from progesterone-mediated sphincter relaxation and does not predict complications.
D. "Forget" (forgetfulness) is a garbled recall option with no prognostic value in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Vaginal bleeding is the most important warning symptom in pregnancy.
  • First trimester bleeding: miscarriage, ectopic
  • Painful antepartum bleeding: abruption
  • Painless antepartum bleeding: previa
  • Heartburn, ankle edema: usually physiological
exam_pearl: In recurrent pregnancy loss, bleeding outranks pain: pain without bleeding is nonspecific, while any bleeding needs urgent ultrasound.

stem: Pregnant, GA about 24 weeks; they found out that the patient didn't receive rubella vaccine. When should the pregnant woman receive MMR?
why_right: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy. A rubella non-immune woman found at 24 weeks is vaccinated postpartum, before discharge, to protect future pregnancies from congenital rubella syndrome. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication, and she should avoid conceiving for about 4 weeks after the dose.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 28 weeks she is still pregnant, so the live vaccine is still contraindicated; there is no safe window during pregnancy.
C. She is non-immune, so vaccination is needed to prevent rubella and congenital rubella syndrome in future pregnancies; meanwhile she should avoid contact with rubella cases.
D. Giving a live vaccine now is contraindicated; note that inadvertent rubella vaccination in pregnancy is not an indication for termination, as outcomes are usually favorable.
key_concept:
Rubella non-immune in pregnancy: avoid exposure now, vaccinate after delivery.
  • Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) given preconception or postpartum
  • Avoid pregnancy for about 4 weeks after MMR
  • Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to MMR
  • Accidental vaccination in pregnancy: counsel, do not terminate
exam_pearl: Non-immune pregnant woman: the answer is never "vaccinate now"; it is "postpartum".
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall note (translated from Arabic): option B was worded as 'don't take it now, take it later'.

stem: Girl came complaining of irregular cycle and hirsutism. On examination only there is hirsutism. Lab tests of TSH, dehydroepiandrosterone, testosterone only done and all are normal. What is the management?
why_right: Irregular cycles plus hirsutism with normal TSH and normal androgens (excluding thyroid disease and androgen-secreting tumor) fits PCOS on clinical grounds, and no fertility wish is stated. The combined oral contraceptive pill is first line because it treats both complaints: it regulates cycles and protects the endometrium, and it suppresses ovarian androgen production and raises SHBG to improve hirsutism.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spironolactone is a second-line antiandrogen added when hirsutism persists on the combined pill; it does not regulate cycles and is teratogenic, so it needs reliable contraception.
B. Clomiphene induces ovulation; it is used only when the woman wants to conceive, which is not the case here.
C. Progestogen-only pills give endometrial protection and withdrawal bleeds but do not reduce androgens, so the hirsutism is untreated.
key_concept:
PCOS treatment depends on the main complaint.
  • All: lifestyle and weight loss
  • Irregular cycles and/or hirsutism, no fertility wish: combined OCP
  • Hirsutism not controlled on OCP: add spironolactone
  • Wants pregnancy: letrozole or clomiphene
  • Insulin resistance: metformin
exam_pearl: The moment the stem adds "wants to conceive", OCP is wrong and ovulation induction is right.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Age missing in the recall ('years old girl'). Related screenshot in the same block: female with signs and symptoms of PCO has hirsutism, facial hair bothering her cosmetically, first line management (no mention of fertility desire)? A. Metformin B. Finasteride C. OCP D. Spironolactone; Answer: C (OCP).

stem: A 17-year-old primigravida presents to the clinic for the first time after missing her period, with a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago. Pelvic examination reveals a closed cervical os with no bleeding (see report). Transvaginal Ultrasound: An intrauterine gestational sac with no embryonic heartbeat. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: closed cervical os with no bleeding
intrauterine gestational sac with no embryonic heartbeat
why_right: Her LMP was "5 weeks ago" and TVUS shows an "intrauterine gestational sac with no embryonic heartbeat". At 5 weeks an absent heartbeat is expected, because cardiac activity usually appears around 6 to 7 weeks. The location is known (intrauterine) but viability cannot yet be judged, so this is an intrauterine pregnancy of uncertain viability, followed by a repeat scan.
why_wrong_block:
A. Inevitable miscarriage needs an open cervical os with products not yet passed. Here the os is "closed" and there is no bleeding.
B. Threatened miscarriage needs vaginal bleeding with a closed os and an ongoing pregnancy. She has "no bleeding".
C. Pregnancy of unknown location applies only when no sac is seen anywhere. Here the sac is clearly intrauterine, so the location is known.
key_concept:
Early scan labels: location first, then viability.
  • No sac anywhere = pregnancy of unknown location
  • Intrauterine sac, too early to confirm heartbeat = IUP of uncertain viability
  • Heartbeat usually visible by about 6 to 7 weeks
  • Bleeding + closed os + viable IUP = threatened miscarriage
  • Plan: repeat TVUS rather than intervene
exam_pearl: No heartbeat at 5 weeks is normal, not a miscarriage; do not call it missed or anembryonic this early.

stem: A Pregnant 17 week female came with goiter and neck mass, TSH was high, T4 low, afraid that her baby become mentally retarded, what's the management?
why_right: High TSH with low T4 is overt primary hypothyroidism; with a goiter in pregnancy this is most often Hashimoto thyroiditis or iodine deficiency. Untreated maternal hypothyroidism impairs fetal neurodevelopment, which is exactly her worry, so the treatment is levothyroxine, started promptly and titrated to trimester-specific TSH targets.
why_wrong_block:
B. Carbimazole is an antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism (low TSH, high T4); it would worsen hypothyroidism and is avoided in the first trimester because of embryopathy.
C. Surgery is for compressive goiter or suspected malignancy, not for hypothyroidism; if needed in pregnancy it is done in the second trimester.
D. Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (it ablates the fetal thyroid) and is a treatment for hyperthyroidism anyway.
key_concept:
Read the TSH direction first, then pick the drug.
  • High TSH, low T4: hypothyroid, give levothyroxine
  • Low TSH, high T4 in first trimester: PTU
  • Low TSH, high T4 after first trimester: carbimazole/methimazole
  • Radioiodine: never in pregnancy
  • Pregnancy raises levothyroxine requirements
exam_pearl: The goiter is a distractor pulling you toward surgery; the labs (high TSH, low T4) decide the answer.

stem: 26-year-old woman, her menarche was at the age of 15 years. Her last cycle was 9 months ago (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Gameboy Hidden Labs: labs showed high FSH (50) and normal LH (37)
why_right: A 26-year-old with 9 months of secondary amenorrhea and a markedly raised FSH (50) has hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: the ovaries have failed, so loss of negative feedback drives FSH up. Ovarian failure before age 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency, and FSH is the most characteristic marker. Management is HRT to relieve estrogen deficiency and protect bone.
why_wrong_block:
A. An ovarian tumor (androgen or estrogen secreting) would suppress gonadotropins or cause virilization, not produce a high FSH ovarian failure picture.
B. Asherman's syndrome causes amenorrhea from intrauterine adhesions after D&C or cesarean, with normal hormone levels; there is no instrumentation history here.
D. PCOS shows normal or low FSH with a raised LH:FSH ratio and hyperandrogenism; a high FSH argues against it.
key_concept:
Secondary amenorrhea: let FSH split the causes.
  • High FSH, low estrogen, age under 40: POI
  • High FSH at age 45 or more with vasomotor symptoms: menopause
  • Low or normal FSH, low LH: hypothalamic or pituitary cause
  • High LH:FSH ratio with hyperandrogenism: PCOS
  • Normal hormones, no bleed to E+P challenge, after D&C: Asherman
exam_pearl: Same high FSH in a 48-year-old is menopause; in a woman under 40 it is POI.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presented with heavy vaginal bleeding (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A "44-year-old" with "heavy vaginal bleeding" and abnormal labs (implying significant blood loss) is treated as severe acute AUB. Dilatation and curettage stops severe bleeding quickly and also provides endometrial tissue, which is needed in a woman in her 40s to exclude hyperplasia or malignancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hysterectomy: definitive surgery for chronic AUB refractory to treatment when childbearing is complete; not the next step in an acute bleed without a tissue diagnosis.
B. Mefenamic acid: an NSAID that reduces chronic heavy menstrual bleeding; too weak for severe acute bleeding.
C. Insert hormonal IUD: the LNG IUD is a first line option for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding, not for acute severe bleeding, and it gives no tissue diagnosis.
key_concept:
Acute AUB ladder:
  • Stabilize: ABC, IV access, transfuse if needed
  • Medical: IV estrogen, high dose COCP or oral progestin, tranexamic acid
  • Severe, unstable or refractory: D&C (therapeutic + diagnostic)
  • Chronic HMB: LNG IUD, COCP, NSAIDs, tranexamic acid
  • Refractory chronic, family complete: ablation or hysterectomy
exam_pearl: Heavy acute bleeding in a woman over 40: D&C both stops the bleed and samples the endometrium.
compiler_note: Compiler note: GB ✅ D (Gameboy). Option D also highlighted.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 6 weeks gestation is receiving methotrexate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy. The first dose of methotrexate 50 mg/m IM was administered one week ago. The human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels on days 1, 4, and 7 were as follows: Day 1: 1000 mIU/mL Day 4: 1200 mIU/mL Day 7: 800 mIU/mL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptC: Administer a second dose of methotrexate
why_right: From day 4 (1200) to day 7 (800) hCG falls by about one third, well above the 15% threshold, so the single dose of methotrexate is working. The plan is repeat beta-hCG weekly until it becomes undetectable. The day 1 to day 4 rise is an expected early effect and does not count as failure.
why_wrong_block:
B. Immediate surgery is for a rising hCG after methotrexate or for rupture or instability; this hCG is falling appropriately.
C. A second methotrexate dose is given only when the day 4 to day 7 fall is less than 15% or hCG plateaus.
D. A multiple-dose regimen is not needed when the response to a single dose is adequate.
key_concept:
After single-dose methotrexate, judge the response on the day 4 vs day 7 hCG, never day 1 vs day 7.
  • Day 1 to day 4 rise: expected, ignore
  • Fall >15% (day 4 to 7): weekly hCG until undetectable
  • Plateau or fall <15%: second methotrexate dose
  • Rising hCG: treatment failure, surgery (laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingostomy)
  • Unstable or signs of rupture at any point: immediate surgery
exam_pearl: Same numbers on days 1 and 4 across these variants; only the day 7 value decides the answer.

stem: A case of a 45 year-old female patient of 35 weeks gestational age. Scheduled for C/S. Taking her pregnancy vitamins. Her BMI is 31. No risk of VTE mentioned. What should be her VTE prophylaxis?
OptB: Continue her vitamins and no prophylaxis needed
why_right: "No risk of VTE mentioned" is the trap: she actually has several risk factors, namely age 45, BMI 31 (obesity) and a planned cesarean delivery, on top of pregnancy itself. Combined risk factors justify pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH (enoxaparin) around and after the cesarean, plus mechanical prophylaxis with compression stockings.
why_wrong_block:
B. "No prophylaxis" ignores her risk factors; it fits only a low-risk woman having a vaginal delivery who is mobile.
C. Early ambulation is encouraged for every woman after delivery but is not sufficient alone when several VTE risk factors coexist.
D. Low-dose aspirin in pregnancy is used for preeclampsia prevention, not as VTE prophylaxis; LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Assess every pregnant woman for VTE risk; prophylaxis scales with the number of risk factors.
  • Risk factors: age over 35, obesity, cesarean delivery, multiple pregnancy, preeclampsia, thrombophilia, prior VTE, immobility
  • Several risk factors: LMWH plus mechanical methods
  • Drug of choice in pregnancy: LMWH (warfarin and DOACs avoided)
  • Aspirin: preeclampsia prevention, not VTE
exam_pearl: Count the hidden risk factors (age, BMI, cesarean) even when the stem says none are mentioned.
