stem: A 24-week pregnant woman presents with exertional dyspnea. She is otherwise healthy, and systemic examination is unremarkable. Ultrasound shows monochorionic twin pregnancy with evidence of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptC: Laser photocoagulation of placental vascular anastomoses
why_right: TTTS in monochorionic twins arises from unbalanced vascular anastomoses on the shared placenta; untreated progressive disease carries very high perinatal mortality. At 24 weeks (within the roughly 16 to 26 week window) the definitive treatment is fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the anastomoses, which treats the cause and improves survival and neurological outcome. Her exertional dyspnea fits uterine overdistension from polyhydramnios in the recipient twin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Termination is not the standard answer when an effective fetal therapy exists; it is a counselling option in severe or late-detected disease only.
B. Expectant observation with close ultrasound surveillance is reasonable only for early, stable disease (Quintero stage I); established TTTS needs laser.
D. Cesarean at 24 weeks means extreme prematurity; delivery is considered only at later gestations or when fetal therapy is not possible.
key_concept:
TTTS: monochorionic twins, donor (oligohydramnios, small bladder) vs recipient (polyhydramnios, overload).
  • Stage I, stable: close surveillance
  • Stage II to IV, roughly 16 to 26 weeks: fetoscopic laser ablation
  • Beyond the laser window: amnioreduction, then delivery planning
  • Screen monochorionic twins with ultrasound every 2 weeks from 16 weeks
exam_pearl: Dichorionic twins cannot get TTTS; the key word is "monochorionic".
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0084).

stem: Newly married women came to preconception clinic, know hx of chronic HTN controlled with lifestyle modification, want to conceive in the next few months Her BP 150/95 What appropriate step (sth like this not sure)?
OptB: Give aspirin to prevent pre eclampsia
OptC: Start antihypertensive treatment to control BP before conception
OptD: Postpone pregnancy until BP level stabilized
highlight_terms_source: chronic HTN controlled with lifestyle modification
why_right: She has known chronic hypertension and is planning pregnancy within months, yet lifestyle measures have failed: BP is still 150/95. Preconception care aims to have the disease controlled before conception, so the right step is to start (or switch to) an antihypertensive that is safe in pregnancy, such as labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa, and then let her conceive with BP controlled.
why_wrong_block:
A. Continuing lifestyle modification alone is reasonable only while BP is at target; at 150/95 it has clearly failed, and uncontrolled BP at conception raises the risk of superimposed pre-eclampsia and growth restriction.
B. Low-dose aspirin is indicated for chronic hypertension, but it is started during pregnancy from about 12 weeks, not before conception, and it does not treat her current BP.
D. Hypertension is not a reason to postpone pregnancy indefinitely; it is treated so she can conceive safely. Delay alone does nothing to lower BP.
key_concept:
Chronic disease preconception: optimise control with pregnancy-safe drugs, then conceive.
  • Safe antihypertensives: labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs: stop or switch (fetal renal toxicity)
  • Aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention: start from about 12 weeks of pregnancy
  • Folic acid preconception for all
exam_pearl: If she were already on an ACE inhibitor, the answer becomes 'switch to a pregnancy-safe agent', not 'start treatment'.

stem: Patient in labor, everything normal GA 33, head felt in vagina (didn't mention +2 or less)
why_right: The head is low ("felt in vagina"), so if delivery has to be assisted an instrument is possible rather than a CS. The decisive clue is GA 33 weeks: the vacuum is avoided in preterm babies because of the risk of scalp injury and intracranial or subgaleal bleeding, so forceps is the instrument of choice before 34 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ventouse is the usual first instrument at term, but it is avoided below 34 weeks because the preterm skull is soft and prone to cephalhematoma and intracranial hemorrhage.
C. CS is for a high head (above +2 station), not fully dilated, fetal distress remote from delivery or malpresentation; with the head already in the vagina, vaginal delivery is quicker and safer.
D. Fetal scalp blood sampling assesses suspected hypoxia on an abnormal CTG; it is not a delivery method and is avoided in preterm fetuses.
key_concept:
Instrument choice depends on station and gestation.
  • Fully dilated + head at +2 or lower: instrumental delivery possible
  • Head above +2: CS
  • Term: ventouse or forceps
  • Preterm below 34 weeks: forceps, avoid ventouse
  • Face presentation (mento-anterior): forceps, not ventouse
exam_pearl: Same low head at term gives ventouse or forceps; the preterm gestation is what rules out the ventouse.

stem: A 22 years old woman with a history of multiple sexual transmitted diseases presented at the 37th gestational week for her first antenatal visit. The obstetrician is concerned about this maternal infection which may cause conjunctivitis and blindness in the newborn. Which of the following is the most suitable for health promotion and illness prevention?
highlight_terms_source: conjunctivitis and blindness in the newborn
why_right: Maternal genital infections that cause neonatal conjunctivitis and blindness are Chlamydia and gonorrhea, acquired during vaginal birth. She has a history of multiple STIs and is at 37 weeks with no antenatal care, so prevention means treating the mother before delivery. Azithromycin is the pregnancy-safe treatment for Chlamydia (gonorrhea is covered by adding ceftriaxone), which removes the source before the baby passes through the birth canal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance ignores a high-risk woman with a transmissible infection; it fits only a low-risk patient with negative screening.
C. Screening the newborn after delivery is too late to prevent exposure; neonatal eye prophylaxis and treatment are added on, but the preventive step is treating the mother first.
D. Referral delays treatment at 37 weeks when delivery is imminent; uncomplicated Chlamydia or gonorrhea is treated directly by the obstetrician.
key_concept:
Ophthalmia neonatorum: prevent by treating the mother before delivery.
  • Gonococcal: early (first days), purulent, can perforate cornea and cause blindness; ceftriaxone
  • Chlamydial: later (about 1 to 2 weeks), most common; azithromycin in pregnancy
  • Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy
  • Newborn: routine eye prophylaxis; treat Chlamydia conjunctivitis with oral erythromycin
exam_pearl: Health promotion/prevention wording points to treating the mother now, not screening or treating the newborn later.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0264).

stem: 45 yr old Female patient with PCOS asking about what is her high risk for developing endometrial cancer:
why_right: PCOS causes chronic anovulation, so there is no corpus luteum and no progesterone to oppose estrogen. Unopposed estrogen drives endometrial proliferation, then hyperplasia, then carcinoma. In a 45 year old (still premenopausal), PCOS is the strongest risk factor offered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Age does raise risk, but most endometrial cancers occur after menopause; at 45 she is below the peak age, so her PCOS outweighs it. Age would be the answer for an older postmenopausal woman without other risk factors.
C. Multiparity is protective, because pregnancy brings long progesterone-dominant intervals; nulliparity is the risk factor.
key_concept:
Endometrial cancer = excess or unopposed estrogen.
  • Obesity (peripheral aromatase), PCOS, anovulation
  • Nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause
  • Unopposed estrogen therapy, tamoxifen
  • Diabetes, Lynch syndrome
  • Protective: progestins, combined OCP, multiparity, smoking
exam_pearl: If the option were nulliparity or obesity in a PCOS patient, think one mechanism: unopposed estrogen.

stem: Pregnant presented with severe abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding. 33 gestational week, she was hypotensive, ctg is reassurance, her bleeding did not stopped since admission. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptD: immediate CS after one dose of dexa
why_right: Severe abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding is placental abruption. The decisive clues are maternal: she is hypotensive and the bleeding has not stopped, so the mother is unstable. An unstable mother with abruption is delivered by CS regardless of fetal status, even with a reassuring CTG. At 33 weeks a dose of dexamethasone can be given on the way, but it must not delay delivery.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood transfusion is part of resuscitation and should run alongside, but it does not stop the bleeding; only delivering the placenta does.
B. Induction is for a stable mother (especially with IUFD) where vaginal delivery can be awaited; an unstable, bleeding mother cannot wait for labor to progress.
C. Steroids with observation (expectant care) fits a stable mother with a reassuring fetus below 34 weeks; ongoing bleeding with hypotension rules it out.
key_concept:
Abruption management depends on mother, fetus and gestation.
  • Unstable mother (any fetal status): CS
  • Stable mother, non-reassuring fetus: CS
  • Stable mother, IUFD: induction / vaginal delivery
  • Stable, reassuring, below 34 weeks: admit, steroids (MgSO4 below 32 weeks), expectant
  • Stable, reassuring, at or near term: deliver, vaginally if possible
exam_pearl: Reassuring CTG does not buy time when the mother is hypotensive and still bleeding; maternal instability decides.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q (other version): 33 wks GA Pregnant presented with moderate vaginal bleeding, she was hypotensive (SBP 60) and high HR.

stem: 38wk GA, present with abdominal pain and vaginal bleed (case of placental abruption), BP 90/60 and HR 100, (no symptoms of shock were reported). She was in active labor with 4 cm dilation, and the fetal head is engaged, CTG was reassuring and fetal was not in any distress. What is management?
why_right: This recall's key is immediate CS because the vitals (BP 90/60, HR 100) are read as maternal hemodynamic compromise from the abruption, and an abruption with an unstable mother is delivered by CS regardless of fetal status or labor progress. Abruption bleeding is often partly concealed, so these numbers may understate the blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
B. Amniotomy is the classic step for an abruption at term in a hemodynamically stable mother with a reassuring fetus in labor: it lowers intrauterine pressure and speeds vaginal delivery. The key rejects it because the mother is treated as unstable.
C. Amniotomy plus oxytocin is used when a stable mother's labor needs augmentation; it relies on time that a compromised, bleeding mother may not have.
key_concept:
Abruption at term: the mother's stability chooses the route.
  • Unstable mother: CS
  • Non-reassuring fetus (not about to deliver): CS
  • Stable mother + reassuring fetus in labor: amniotomy ± oxytocin, vaginal delivery
  • IUFD + stable mother: vaginal delivery
exam_pearl: Same scenario with clearly normal vitals points to amniotomy; borderline hypotension with tachycardia is what the key uses to choose CS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot inside the 449 block; the screenshot's answer line reads '- Immediate CS'.

stem: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman with a family history of ovarian cancer presents for evaluation and screening. She is currently asymptomatic and has no known genetic testing. What is the most appropriate next step in her management?
OptC: Counseling and ask about ovarian cancer symptoms
why_right: She is asymptomatic and there is no proven screening test for ovarian cancer: routine pelvic ultrasound and CA-125 in asymptomatic women do not reduce mortality and cause false positives and unnecessary surgery. With a family history and no genetic testing, the right step is counseling: assess her family risk (with referral for genetic counseling and BRCA testing if it fits) and teach her the warning symptoms such as bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain and weight loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pelvic (transvaginal) ultrasound is the first test when there are symptoms or a palpable mass; as a screening test in an asymptomatic woman it is not recommended.
B. CA-125 is used to assess a known adnexal mass or monitor epithelial ovarian cancer; it is not sensitive or specific enough for screening (raised in endometriosis, fibroids, PID).
D. CEA is mainly a colorectal cancer marker (and sometimes raised in mucinous ovarian tumors); it has no role in ovarian cancer screening.
key_concept:
Ovarian cancer: no effective screening test.
  • Asymptomatic, family history: risk assessment, genetic counseling, symptom awareness
  • Symptoms or mass: TVUS first, then CA-125
  • Confirmed BRCA carrier: risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing
  • Diagnosis: tissue histopathology; staging is surgical
exam_pearl: Symptoms or a mass flip the answer to TVUS then CA-125; without them, screening tests are a trap.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: 'Post menopause with a family history of ovarian cancer comes for screening for ovarian cancer. What do you do for her?' (options Pelvic US / CA125 / Counseling), Answer: C. Fuller Q version highlights C.

stem: A pregnant lady at 26 weeks, she cannot feel fetal movement anymore. US showed: IUFD at age of 24 weeks. Best management:
why_right: Fetal death at or after 20 weeks is IUFD, and here it occurred at 24 weeks. The preferred route is vaginal delivery by induction, and in the second and early third trimester the cervix is unripe and the uterus is relatively insensitive to oxytocin, so misoprostol (often after mifepristone) is the agent of choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV oxytocin works poorly at this gestation because uterine oxytocin receptors are few and the cervix is unripe; it is used near term or once the cervix is favorable.
B. CS adds surgical morbidity and scars the uterus for no fetal benefit; it is reserved for maternal indications such as abruption with instability, uterine rupture or transverse lie that cannot be corrected.
D. D&C is limited to losses up to about 20 weeks (miscarriage); a 24-week fetus is too large and the uterus would be at high risk of perforation.
key_concept:
Pregnancy loss: route depends on gestation.
  • Below 13 weeks: expectant, misoprostol or D&C
  • Up to 20 weeks: misoprostol or D&C (D&C if heavy bleeding or unstable)
  • IUFD (20 weeks or more): induce vaginal delivery, misoprostol ± mifepristone
  • Near term with favorable cervix: oxytocin
  • Check coagulation (risk of DIC with retained dead fetus)
exam_pearl: Gestation is the trap: D&C fits a miscarriage below 20 weeks, oxytocin fits term; 24 weeks means misoprostol.

stem: A 21-year-old woman pregnant at 8 weeks is diagnosed with a missed abortion. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
why_right: A missed abortion at "8 weeks" in a stable patient can be managed expectantly (if under 13 weeks), medically with misoprostol (up to 20 weeks), or surgically. Expectant management is not offered here, so misoprostol is the most appropriate option: it is effective, avoids surgery and is the standard medical evacuation agent.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hysterectomy is far too radical for an early miscarriage in a young woman; evacuation is achieved medically or by suction curettage.
C. Methotrexate is used for ectopic pregnancy and post-molar GTN, not for an intrauterine missed abortion.
D. Hypertonic saline infusion is an obsolete intra-amniotic method of second-trimester termination; it has no role at 8 weeks.
key_concept:
Missed abortion (closed os, no fetal heart, no tissue passed): choose by stability and gestation.
  • <13 weeks, stable: expectant management is an option
  • Up to 20 weeks: misoprostol (medical)
  • Heavy bleeding, instability or infection: D&C / suction evacuation
  • Methotrexate: ectopic or GTN only
exam_pearl: If expectant management is listed for a stable early missed abortion, pick it; if it is absent, pick misoprostol.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot (source Q 0391) shown inside the 451 block.

stem: 39 weeks, I think she is not primigravida, her cervix is 4 cm dilated with strong and regular contraction, after 4 hours the cervix dilated to 5 cm, fully effaced cervix (if you calculate the bishop score it would be favorable). What is the management?
why_right: She has strong, regular contractions but progressed only from 4 to 5 cm in 4 hours, which is slower than expected (less than 2 cm in 4 hours) yet is not arrest, because the cervix did change. With intact membranes and adequate contractions, the first step for delay in the first stage is amniotomy, then reassess in about 2 hours.
why_wrong_block:
A. CS for failure to progress needs arrest: no cervical change despite adequate contractions over the defined time (or failed augmentation). Here the cervix is still changing and the fetus is well.
B. Oxytocin is for inadequate contractions or for delay that persists after amniotomy; her contractions are already strong and regular, so adding oxytocin first risks tachysystole.
D. Waiting another 2 hours is right when progress is normal (about 1 cm in 2 hours); 1 cm in 4 hours is delay that needs action.
key_concept:
Slow first stage: ladder of action.
  • Normal progress (about 0.5 cm/hour): reassess
  • Delay with intact membranes: amniotomy, reassess in 2 hours
  • Still slow or weak contractions: oxytocin
  • No change despite adequate contractions or failed oxytocin: CS
exam_pearl: If the same 1 cm gain had taken only 2 hours, progress would be normal and the answer becomes reassess in 2 hours.

stem: 39 weeks, I think she is not primigravida, her cervix is 4 cm dilated with strong and regular contraction, after 2 hours the cervix dilated to 5 cm, fully effaced cervix (if you calculate the bishop score it would be favorable). What is the management?
why_right: Progress from 4 to 5 cm in 2 hours equals about 0.5 cm per hour, which is normal for the first stage. With strong, regular contractions, a fully effaced cervix and no fetal concern, labor is progressing and no intervention is needed: reassess in 2 hours.
why_wrong_block:
A. CS is for arrest of labor or fetal or maternal compromise; she is progressing normally.
B. Oxytocin augments weak or inadequate contractions or persistent delay; her contractions are already strong, so it adds risk of tachysystole without benefit.
C. Amniotomy is the first step when progress is delayed (less than 2 cm in 4 hours); routine amniotomy in normally progressing labor is not recommended.
key_concept:
First-stage progress check.
  • About 0.5 cm/hour (1 cm in 2 hours): normal, reassess
  • Less than 2 cm in 4 hours: delay, amniotomy then reassess in 2 hours
  • Weak contractions or persistent delay: oxytocin
  • No change with adequate contractions: CS
exam_pearl: If the same 1 cm gain had taken 4 hours, that is delay and the answer becomes amniotomy.

stem: A 22-year-old primigravida woman at 38 weeks gestation is in active labor for 4 hours. Cervical dilatation is 5 cm, +1 station. Examination 5 hours later demonstrates no change compared to the previous findings. Contractions occur every 3 minutes and lasts 60 seconds. Fetal heart rate is of category 1 cardiotocograph. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: Contractions occur every 3 minutes and lasts 60 seconds
why_right: At 5 cm she is in the active phase. Contractions every 3 minutes lasting 60 seconds fall within the adequate range (3 to 5 per 10 minutes), yet the cervix has shown no change for 5 hours. Adequate contractions for 4 hours or more without cervical change is active phase arrest, which is an indication for cesarean section.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin augmentation is for INADEQUATE contractions with no change over 6 hours; her contractions are already adequate, so more uterotonic only risks tachysystole without fixing the arrest.
C. Waiting is right in the latent phase or before the arrest window is reached; here the 4 hour limit with adequate contractions has already passed, so the diagnosis of arrest is made now.
D. Instrumental delivery needs full cervical dilatation with the head at +2 or lower; she is only 5 cm at +1 station.
key_concept:
Active phase arrest: decide by contraction adequacy.
  • Active phase: cervix beyond 4 to 6 cm
  • Adequate = 3 to 5 contractions per 10 min
  • Adequate contractions + no change ≥4 h → C-section
  • Inadequate contractions + no change ≥6 h → oxytocin, then C-section if it fails
  • Instrumental delivery only at full dilatation, head ≥ +2
exam_pearl: Normal (Category 1) CTG does not remove the indication: the C-section here is for arrest of labor, not fetal distress.

stem: 35 weeks gestation, abdomen fundal examination corresponds to 30 cm. Ruptured membrane for 6h, she is stable, no Uterine contractions. Upon vaginal examination, meconium stained liquor found
OptD: Prophylactic Abx and observation for spontaneous delivery
why_right: Membranes ruptured before labor at 35 weeks is PPROM; beyond 34 weeks the fetal lungs and brain are mature enough that delivery is favoured over expectant management. Meconium-stained liquor and a fundal height of only 30 cm at 35 weeks (small for dates) add further reasons to deliver, while a stable mother and no fetal distress mean vaginal delivery can be attempted. With rupture only 6 hours ago, this recall's key is induction alone; its twin card with 16 hours of rupture adds antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cesarean section is for fetal distress (non-reassuring CTG), malpresentation or obstructed labor; meconium alone in a stable patient does not mandate it.
C. Induction plus prophylactic antibiotics is this recall's answer once rupture is prolonged (the 16 hour version of this question); at 6 hours the key gives induction alone.
D. Waiting for spontaneous labor fits PPROM below 34 weeks to gain maturity; at 35 weeks with meconium and a small-for-dates uterus there is no benefit to waiting, only infection risk.
key_concept:
PPROM: gestational age sets the plan.
  • <32 wk: MgSO4 for neuroprotection
  • <34 wk: steroids + latency antibiotics, expectant if stable
  • ≥34 wk: deliver (induction if no contraindication to vaginal birth)
  • Deliver at any age if chorioamnionitis, abruption, non-reassuring CTG
  • Fundal height in cm ≈ weeks of gestation; a big lag suggests growth restriction
exam_pearl: Same stem, different hours: short rupture = induce; longer rupture = induce + antibiotics.

stem: 35 weeks gestation, abdomen fundal examination corresponds to 30 cm. Ruptured membrane for 16h, she is stable, no Uterine contractions. Upon vaginal examination, meconium stained liquor found
OptD: Prophylactic Abx and observation for spontaneous delivery
why_right: At 35 weeks with membranes ruptured before labor (PPROM), delivery is favoured beyond 34 weeks, and meconium-stained liquor with a small-for-dates uterus (30 cm) strengthens that. Prolonged rupture (16 hours) in a preterm pregnancy raises the risk of ascending infection, and preterm delivery with unknown GBS status is itself an indication for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis, so antibiotics are added while labor is induced. The mother is stable with no fetal distress, so vaginal delivery is attempted.
why_wrong_block:
A. Induction alone is this recall's answer when rupture is short (the 6 hour twin); with 16 hours of rupture in a preterm pregnancy, antibiotic cover is added.
B. Cesarean is for fetal distress, malpresentation or obstructed labor; meconium in a stable patient without CTG abnormality is not an indication.
D. Expectant management with antibiotics fits PPROM below 34 weeks; at 35 weeks with meconium, waiting adds infection risk without benefit.
key_concept:
PPROM ≥34 weeks: deliver, cover infection.
  • <34 wk stable: steroids + latency antibiotics + expectant care
  • ≥34 wk: induce labor
  • Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis: GBS positive, or status unknown with preterm (<37 wk), rupture ≥18 h or fever
  • Chorioamnionitis: antibiotics + deliver at any gestation
  • C-section only for obstetric indications
exam_pearl: The only difference from the 6 hour twin is rupture duration: longer rupture adds antibiotics.

stem: A 37 weeks GA came to the labor room with PROM for 24 hours, how to prevent postpartum pelvic infection?
why_right: PROM for 24 hours lets vaginal flora ascend, and postpartum pelvic infection (endometritis) is polymicrobial: anaerobes plus gram-negative aerobes. Clindamycin plus gentamicin covers both groups and is the classic regimen for postpartum uterine infection, which is why this recall keys it for preventing pelvic infection after prolonged rupture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms (used for MRSA or GBS in severe penicillin allergy) and misses the anaerobes and gram-negatives of pelvic infection.
B. Clindamycin alone covers anaerobes and some gram-positives but leaves gram-negative aerobes (E. coli) uncovered; gentamicin is added for that.
D. Amoxicillin plus metronidazole covers anaerobes and many gram-positives, but amoxicillin alone gives unreliable cover of the gram-negative aerobes (E. coli is often resistant), which is the gap gentamicin fills.
key_concept:
Obstetric infection regimens.
  • Chorioamnionitis: ampicillin + gentamicin, then deliver
  • After cesarean: add clindamycin for anaerobes
  • Postpartum endometritis: clindamycin + gentamicin
  • PPROM latency: ampicillin + erythromycin
  • Term PROM: deliver within 24 h; GBS prophylaxis if positive or unknown
exam_pearl: Pelvic infection is polymicrobial: you need anaerobe cover (clindamycin) AND gram-negative cover (gentamicin).

stem: A 42-year-old woman presented with pelvic pressure, bloating, and heaviness in the lower abdomen. Her cycle is prolonged with heavy menstrual bleeding (see report). Ultrasound: Presence of uterine fibroid. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clue is the combination: pressure, bloating and heaviness PLUS prolonged heavy menstrual bleeding with a fibroid on ultrasound. A submucosal fibroid distorts the endometrial cavity, so it is the type that causes heavy bleeding (and infertility) in addition to bulk symptoms. Pressure alone could be any location; the bleeding makes it submucosal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cervical fibroid: rare; gives bladder or bowel pressure, dyspareunia or obstructed labor rather than classic heavy menstrual bleeding.
B. Parasitic fibroid: a pedunculated subserosal fibroid that detaches and takes blood supply from omentum or other structures; causes pressure or a mass effect, not menorrhagia.
C. Subserosal fibroid: the commonest type, but it projects outward and causes pressure or heaviness only; it would be the answer if the stem had pressure WITHOUT heavy bleeding.
key_concept:
Fibroid location is predicted by symptoms: bleeding means the cavity is involved.
  • Submucosal: heavy menstrual bleeding + infertility + pressure
  • Intramural: pressure or heaviness (bleeding if large)
  • Subserosal: pressure or heaviness only; most common type
  • Ultrasound (TVUS) is the initial and diagnostic test
  • Submucosal myomectomy is hysteroscopic
exam_pearl: Menorrhagia with a fibroid = submucosal; pressure symptoms alone do not decide the type.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presented with heavy menorrhagia and pelvic pressure with Lower limb heaviness and edema. Pelvic ultrasound confirms the presence of uterine fibroid. What is the most likely location of this fibroid?
why_right: This recall's key is Intramural because the picture combines heavy menorrhagia with bulk effects: pelvic pressure and lower limb heaviness and edema, which suggest a large fibroid compressing pelvic veins. Intramural fibroids sit in the muscle wall, enlarge the uterus and the endometrial surface, so they can produce both heavy bleeding and pressure symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cervical fibroids are rare; they cause local pressure effects (urinary or bowel symptoms, obstructed labor) rather than heavy menstrual bleeding.
B. Subserosal fibroids grow outward and cause pressure or heaviness but typically NOT menorrhagia, so they do not explain her bleeding.
D. Submucosal fibroids are the classic cause of menorrhagia and infertility; pick them when bleeding dominates without marked bulk symptoms such as leg edema.
key_concept:
Fibroid location by symptom.
  • Submucosal: menorrhagia, infertility, (pressure)
  • Intramural: bulky uterus, pressure, can increase bleeding
  • Subserosal: pressure/heaviness, little bleeding
  • Cervical: rare, urinary/bowel symptoms, obstructed labor
  • Ultrasound is the initial and diagnostic test
exam_pearl: Menorrhagia alone = submucosal; menorrhagia plus large-mass pressure effects (leg edema) is how this recall points to intramural.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1881).

stem: Patient (32 years old i think) had menorrhagia she had subserosal fibroid 3x3 cm what is the management
why_right: A subserosal fibroid grows outward from the uterus and does not distort the cavity, so it is unlikely to be the cause of her menorrhagia. At only 3x3 cm it is far below the surgical threshold, so the bleeding is treated medically first, and NSAIDs reduce menstrual blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is for a fibroid larger than 7 cm or failed medical treatment in a woman wanting fertility; removing a small subserosal fibroid would not treat bleeding it is not causing.
B. Hysterectomy is definitive surgery for a large symptomatic fibroid in a woman who has completed her family; far too radical for a young woman with a small fibroid.
C. Uterine artery embolization is for a symptomatic surgical candidate who refuses surgery; here the fibroid is not the cause and surgery is not indicated.
key_concept:
Fibroid treatment ladder.
  • Asymptomatic/incidental: observe, yearly ultrasound
  • Symptomatic: medical first (NSAIDs, OCP)
  • GnRH analogue: pre-operative shrinkage
  • Surgery: >7 cm or failed medical treatment
  • Myomectomy if fertility wanted; hysterectomy if family complete
  • UAE: surgical candidate refusing surgery
exam_pearl: Subserosal fibroid + menorrhagia: the fibroid is not the culprit, so treat the bleeding medically.

stem: 32-year-old single woman is attending the clinic complaining of menorrhagia for the last few months. The physical examination is unremarkable. Pelvic Ultrasound: Presence of a serosal fibroid, 4 x 4 cm in size. Otherwise, the other parameters of the ultrasound were normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Her menorrhagia is not explained by the fibroid: a serosal (subserosal) fibroid grows outward and does not distort the cavity, so it rarely causes heavy bleeding, and at 4 x 4 cm it is below the surgical threshold. With a normal examination, the bleeding is treated medically first, and NSAIDs reduce menstrual blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is for fibroids above 7 cm or failed medical therapy; removing a serosal fibroid would not treat bleeding it is not causing.
B. Hysterectomy is far too radical for a young single woman with a small fibroid unrelated to her symptoms, and ends fertility.
C. Embolization is for a symptomatic fibroid needing surgery in a woman who refuses it; here the fibroid is not the cause.
key_concept:
Ask first whether the fibroid explains the symptom.
  • Submucosal: menorrhagia, infertility
  • Intramural: can cause heavy bleeding when large
  • Subserosal: pressure symptoms, rarely bleeding
  • Bleeding not explained by the fibroid: medical treatment (NSAIDs, OCP)
  • Surgery: above 7 cm or failed medical therapy
exam_pearl: Serosal fibroid + menorrhagia = do not blame the fibroid; treat the bleeding medically.

stem: A 39 weeks pregnant female, on examination amniotic fluid was noted to have a dark green color. What's the most appropriate action to be done [[[DURING]]] delivery?
OptC: Oropharyngeal suction before delivering the rest of body
why_right: Dark green amniotic fluid at 39 weeks means meconium-stained liquor, which risks meconium aspiration. This recall's key reflects the traditional teaching for the moment during delivery: suction the mouth and pharynx after the head delivers and before the shoulders and body, aiming to clear meconium before the first breath. Current neonatal resuscitation guidance no longer recommends this routinely; see the concern note.
why_wrong_block:
A. NICU transfer is a post-delivery decision based on the baby's condition; a vigorous baby stays with the mother, and it is not an action during delivery.
B. Immediate intubation for tracheal suction was once advised for a NON-vigorous baby after birth; it is not done during delivery and is no longer routine even then.
D. IV antibiotics treat suspected chorioamnionitis (maternal fever, tachycardia, tender uterus); meconium alone is not an infection.
key_concept:

stem: A 25-year-old woman was diagnosed to have a complete abortion at 10 weeks of gestation. The patient is a heavy smoker and smokes more than 20 cigarettes a day. She was not taking any folic acid or dietary supplements. Which of the following is the most likely risk that caused the miscarriage?

The missing folic acid is a deliberate distractor.

  • Other recognized factors: advanced maternal age, heavy alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes or thyroid disease

stem: A woman was trying to conceive, she is asymptomatic, was found to have serosal fibroid 5x5 cm incidentally on pelvic US. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: She is asymptomatic and the fibroid is serosal and 5x5 cm. Subserosal fibroids grow outward and do not distort the cavity, so they are not a recognised cause of infertility, and 5 cm is below the surgical threshold. An asymptomatic fibroid is managed conservatively with annual follow-up ultrasound, and she can keep trying to conceive.
why_wrong_block:
B. Myomectomy needs a fibroid larger than 7 cm, failed medical therapy, or a cavity-distorting (submucosal) fibroid in infertility; none applies here, and surgery adds uterine scarring before pregnancy.
C. OCPs control bleeding from symptomatic fibroids; she has no symptoms and is trying to conceive, so contraception defeats her goal.
D. Uterine artery embolization is for a symptomatic surgical candidate who refuses surgery, and it is avoided in women who want future pregnancy.
key_concept:

  • Asymptomatic: conservative, yearly ultrasound
  • Submucosal distorting cavity: hysteroscopic myomectomy
  • Subserosal: no effect on fertility
  • Surgery: >7 cm or failed medical treatment
  • Avoid UAE if pregnancy desired
exam_pearl: No word 'incidental' is needed: 'asymptomatic' plus a subserosal fibroid under 7 cm is enough for conservative care.

stem: Baby delivered dead at 38 wks (Stillbirth case). Placenta and baby appear normal Which of the following is best to sent for investigations for chromosomal analysis?
why_right: The baby is already delivered as a stillbirth at 38 weeks, so the sample must come from tissue available after birth. Fetal cells die soon after demise and often fail to grow in culture, whereas placental tissue (taken near the cord insertion) stays viable longer and gives the best chance of a successful karyotype or chromosomal microarray.
why_wrong_block:
A. Umbilical cord sampling (cordocentesis) is a prenatal procedure to draw blood from a LIVING fetus, so it has no role after a stillbirth; a cut segment of cord tissue can be sent as a backup, but placental tissue gives the better yield.
B. Amniotic fluid by amniocentesis is the best sample BEFORE delivery when the dead fetus is still in utero; after birth it is no longer available.
C. Fetal cord blood from a stillborn is clotted and its cells are non-viable, so culture usually fails.
key_concept:
Chromosomal testing in fetal death: timing decides the sample.
  • Fetus still in utero: amniocentesis (amniotic fluid), highest yield
  • After delivery: placental tissue near cord insertion
  • Other post-delivery options: cord segment, internal fetal tissue
  • Fetal blood after death: poor yield
exam_pearl: Delivered = placenta; still inside = amniotic fluid.

stem: A patient with absent fetal heartbeat on ultrasound, which of the following is best to use for chromosomal analysis? (A patient with fetal demise: which of the following is best to use for chromosomal analysis?)
why_right: Absent fetal heartbeat on ultrasound means the dead fetus is still in utero. Amniocentesis before delivery gives amniotic fluid cells that remain viable for culture, making it the highest-yield sample for karyotype or microarray in fetal death; it should be offered before induction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Umbilical cord sampling (cordocentesis) samples blood from a LIVING fetus; after demise there is no circulation and the blood is non-viable.
C. Fetal cord blood after death is clotted and its cells do not grow, so it gives a poor yield.
D. Placental tissue is the best sample AFTER the baby is delivered; while the fetus is still in utero, amniotic fluid is obtained first.

exam_pearl: Same options as the stillbirth card: 'absent heartbeat on ultrasound' (still inside) flips the answer to amniotic fluid.

stem: Patient now delivered how to know about the chromosomal analysis from where to take sample
why_right: The lead-in is "now delivered": the fetus is out, so the sample for karyotype comes from fetal tissue directly, and umbilical cord (cord blood or a cord segment) is fetal in origin and easy to obtain at delivery. Prenatal routes are no longer needed once the baby (or stillborn fetus) and placenta are available.
why_wrong_block:
A. "Maternal cord" is not a fetal sample; any maternal tissue or blood gives the mother's karyotype, not the baby's. Maternal blood is used only for cell free fetal DNA screening during pregnancy.
B. Amniotic fluid (amniocentesis) is a prenatal diagnostic route, usually from about 15 weeks; after delivery it is unnecessary and fetal tissue is available directly.
key_concept:
Sample for fetal karyotype depends on timing.
  • First trimester: chorionic villus sampling
  • Second trimester: amniocentesis
  • Later in pregnancy: fetal (cordocentesis) blood
  • After delivery: cord blood or cord segment, placenta, fetal tissue
  • Maternal blood: cell free DNA screening only, not diagnostic
exam_pearl: Read the timing word: "now delivered" removes every invasive prenatal test from the answer list.

stem: mother presented in OPD concerning for decrease fetal movement, at 18 weeks, there was no fetal heart beat, on her previous visit fetus was normal with normal placenta and fetus heart beat. What the next step for diagnosis?
why_right: She reports decreased fetal movement and no fetal heartbeat was found at 18 weeks; the first diagnostic step is ultrasound to confirm or exclude absent fetal cardiac activity. Ultrasound is the test that diagnoses fetal death, and every other investigation follows only once the diagnosis is confirmed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amniocentesis is for fetal karyotype (prenatal diagnosis); it is part of the cause workup after demise is confirmed, not the step that diagnoses it.
B. Placental tissue sampling (CVS or placental karyotype after delivery) looks for a cause such as aneuploidy; it does not establish whether the fetus is alive.
C. Umbilical cord sampling gives fetal blood for karyotype or infection studies; it is invasive and only for cause, never the first diagnostic test.
key_concept:
Suspected fetal death: confirm with ultrasound first, then look for the cause.
  • Ultrasound: absent cardiac activity confirms demise
  • Before 20 weeks: classed as pregnancy loss (abortion); at or after 20 weeks: IUFD
  • Decreased movement at viable age: history, kick count, NST, then US or BPP
  • After confirmation: karyotype (amniotic fluid, placenta, cord), infection screen, coagulation profile
exam_pearl: "Next step for diagnosis" = imaging to confirm; genetic sampling answers "why", not "whether".

stem: Primigravida came to antenatal clinic concerned about having a NTD. She Has Prior History Of Anencephaly. What Is Recommended Folic Acid Dose?
why_right: This recall's key is 1000 micrograms because hydrocephalus on its own is not a neural tube defect, so the history is treated as moderate rather than high risk, where some guidelines use about 1 mg daily. The high dose of 4 to 5 mg is reserved for a true NTD history (previous NTD pregnancy, NTD in the woman or her partner) or drug and medical risk factors.
why_wrong_block:
B. 2000 micrograms is not a recognised folic acid dose tier, so it is never the intended answer.
C. 5000 micrograms (5 mg) is the high risk dose; it becomes right if the stem states a previous NTD pregnancy (for example spina bifida or anencephaly) or an NTD in either parent.
key_concept:
Folic acid dose follows NTD risk tier.
  • Average risk: 0.4 mg daily
  • Moderate risk (some guidelines): about 1 mg daily
  • High risk (previous NTD, woman or partner with NTD, antiepileptics, diabetes, SCD/thalassemia): 4 to 5 mg daily
  • Hydrocephalus alone is not an NTD, but it often accompanies spina bifida
exam_pearl: If the stem converts "hydrocephalus" into "spina bifida" or "previous NTD baby", the answer flips to 5000 micrograms.

stem: Mother On Phenytoin, What Is Folic Acid Dose
why_right: Phenytoin is an enzyme inducing antiepileptic that lowers folate levels and raises NTD risk, which puts her in the high risk group. High risk women need high dose folic acid, 5 mg (5000 micrograms) daily, rather than the standard 0.4 mg.

stem: 37 weeks gestational female having contractions, baby is cephalic, cervix 4cm dilated, baby at 1+ station. Female started bleeding with tender abdomen, ctg normal fetus
why_right: Bleeding with a tender abdomen in labour is placental abruption. At 37 weeks, already labouring (4 cm, station +1, cephalic) with a normal CTG and no maternal instability described, the plan is expedited vaginal delivery, so labour is augmented with oxytocin (with amniotomy) under close fetal and maternal monitoring.
why_wrong_block:
B. Surgical (instrumental) vaginal delivery needs a fully dilated cervix and a low station; at 4 cm it is not possible. It is used in the second stage when delivery must be expedited.
C. Observation is unsafe: an abruption at term should be delivered, as it can extend and cause fetal distress, coagulopathy or hemorrhage. Expectant care is only for a stable preterm abruption (below 34 weeks) with a reassuring fetus.
D. Anesthesia (epidural for analgesia or general for cesarean) does not treat the abruption; cesarean would be chosen if the mother were unstable or the CTG non reassuring, and coagulopathy must be checked before regional block.
key_concept:
Placental abruption: management depends on mother, fetus and gestation.
  • Unstable mother: cesarean section
  • Non reassuring fetus: cesarean section
  • Stable mother, fetal death: vaginal delivery (induction)
  • Stable, reassuring, term or in labour: vaginal delivery, amniotomy plus oxytocin
  • Stable, reassuring, below 34 weeks: admit, steroids, MgSO4 if below 32 weeks
exam_pearl: Abruption plus normal CTG plus stable mother at term = speed up the vaginal birth; a non reassuring CTG flips it to cesarean.

stem: 40 years old pregnant lady, she's in her second pregnancy, her first pregnancy went very well and she has a living child, her past history is unremarkable, she doesn't have any chronic disease, her BMI is 26. She's now in her 12 week of gestation, And she presented now in her first antenatal care visit, which of the following is the best thing to council her about?
OptA: Do a 50 oral glucose tolerance test
OptB: Council her about the current best options for genetic abnormalities or something like the prenatal care screening.
OptC: Give her low dose aspirin to prevent pre-eclampsia.
why_right: At 40 years the main extra risk of this otherwise low risk pregnancy is fetal aneuploidy, and at her 12 week first visit she is in the window for first trimester screening. So the priority counselling is her options for aneuploidy screening and diagnostic testing (combined screening or cell free DNA, then CVS or amniocentesis if needed).
why_wrong_block:
A. A 50 g glucose challenge is routine at 24 to 28 weeks; early testing is for risk factors such as previous GDM or BMI ≥30, and she has a BMI of 26 with an uneventful first pregnancy.
C. Low dose aspirin is for women at high risk of pre-eclampsia (e.g. previous pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, renal disease) or with two or more moderate factors; age 40 alone is a single moderate factor.
D. Tdap is given later in each pregnancy (third trimester, about 27 to 36 weeks), not at the 12 week booking visit.
key_concept:
First antenatal visit at advanced maternal age:
  • Confirm dating with ultrasound
  • Offer aneuploidy screening: first trimester combined test or cell free DNA
  • Positive screen: diagnostic CVS (10 to 13 weeks) or amniocentesis (from 15 weeks)
  • GDM test: 24 to 28 weeks unless previous GDM or obesity
  • Aspirin: one high risk factor or two moderate factors
exam_pearl: Age alone in a healthy parous woman = counsel on genetic screening; add a second risk factor before thinking aspirin.

stem: A 16-week primigravida who is medically free presented to the clinic with fears of delivering a macrosomic baby. Her BMI is 35. What is the appropriate test?
why_right: A BMI of 35 is obesity, a recognised risk factor for gestational diabetes and macrosomia, so she qualifies for glucose testing with an OGTT rather than routine reassurance. The 75 g OGTT is the one step diagnostic test for GDM and is the appropriate test for her concern.
why_wrong_block: A. Fasting glucose alone misses many cases of GDM, because much of pregnancy hyperglycemia is post load; it is not the standard diagnostic test, though a high fasting value can flag overt diabetes.
key_concept:
GDM testing:
  • Routine: 24 to 28 weeks
  • One step: 2 hour 75 g OGTT (diagnostic)
  • Two step: 50 g challenge, then 3 hour 100 g OGTT if positive
  • Risk factors: BMI ≥30, previous GDM, previous macrosomic baby, first degree relative with diabetes, PCOS
  • HbA1c and random glucose are not GDM diagnostic tests
exam_pearl: Obesity plus fear of a big baby = OGTT, not a single fasting glucose.

stem: G2P1 came at 23 weeks of gestation. Completely normal, O+ blood type, all test unremarkable. She Has 2 Prior Uncomplicated Deliveries. She said her mother was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus type 2. She is concerned about her having it as well. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's concern? (They emphasized type 2 diabetes, not gestational)
highlight_terms_source: mother was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus type 2
why_right: She is at 23 weeks, completely normal, with 2 prior uncomplicated deliveries (no previous GDM or macrosomia); a mother with type 2 diabetes alone does not justify early or immediate testing. The right step is the standard screen, a 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks, which is only a week away and also detects diabetes declaring itself in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. HbA1c is not a reliable diagnostic test in pregnancy (red cell turnover lowers it) and misses GDM; it is used to look for pre existing diabetes at booking in high risk women, not for this concern at 23 weeks.
B. A random glucose is neither sensitive nor diagnostic for GDM; it is only useful when classic symptoms of hyperglycemia are present.
D. The 3 hour 100 g OGTT is step 2 of the two step approach, done only after an abnormal 50 g challenge; it is not the first test.
key_concept:
When to screen for GDM:
  • Everyone: 24 to 28 weeks
  • Early (first visit): previous GDM, previous macrosomia, obesity, or several risk factors combined
  • One step: 75 g 2 hour OGTT
  • Two step: 50 g challenge, then 100 g 3 hour OGTT
  • Family history alone: routine timing
exam_pearl: Family history alone keeps her on the routine 24 to 28 week OGTT; a previous GDM or big baby would pull testing earlier.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a leiomyoma associated with heavy menstruation (see image and lab result). [Labs Showed Low Hb And CT Showing Fibroid] Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?

why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is definitive treatment for a symptomatic fibroid in a woman wanting fertility, but operating on a severely anemic patient is unsafe; it follows correction of the anemia.
C. Oral contraceptive pills can reduce bleeding in mild cases, but they do not treat an already low Hb and are a later option.
D. Uterine artery embolization is an alternative definitive option for women who decline surgery; it also comes after the anemia is corrected.

  • Asymptomatic, incidental: observe and follow up
  • Symptomatic with significant anemia: correct anemia first
  • Medical: NSAIDs or tranexamic acid, hormonal options, GnRH agonist before surgery
  • Wants fertility: myomectomy
  • Completed family: hysterectomy
  • Declines surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: "Next step" plus a low Hb = fix the anemia before any procedure.

stem: A 45-years old female in 5th day post-hysterectomy the patient have fever, she does not complain of anything and the wound is clean. What is your next step of measurement?
why_right: This recall's key is medication review because the patient is on day 5 with fever but "does not complain of anything" and the "wound is clean": there are no urinary, chest or wound clues to direct tests. Drug fever is a non-invasive, often overlooked cause to check first in an asymptomatic postoperative patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC and blood cultures are right when the patient looks septic (rigors, tachycardia, hypotension) or has a line or clear source; in a well, asymptomatic patient they are not the first step in this recall.
B. Urinalysis and culture is right for fever with urinary symptoms or a catheter, typically on days 2 to 3; here the patient has no complaints.
C. A chest X-ray is right for cough, dyspnoea, crackles or reduced breath sounds, mostly in the first days after surgery (atelectasis, pneumonia); there are no chest findings here.
key_concept:

  • Day 1: atelectasis
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI, thrombophlebitis
  • Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT
  • After hysterectomy: also vaginal cuff cellulitis or pelvic collection
  • Drug fever: diagnosis of exclusion; patient often looks well
exam_pearl: Symptoms or signs pointing to a source (dysuria, cough, red wound) move the answer to the matching test.

stem: A pregnant woman at 11 weeks gestation is found to have a positive anti-E antibody titer of 1:16. What is the next best step in management ?
key_concept:
Alloimmunized pregnancy: titer first, then Doppler, then treat by gestation.

  • At or above critical titer: stop relying on titers; check paternal antigen status / fetal genotype and start serial MCA Doppler from mid second trimester

  • Hydrops (ascites + skin edema) = severe disease
  • Anti-D prophylaxis only prevents D sensitization in unsensitized women
  • Anti-Kell is the exception: severe anemia even with low titers
