stem: 43-year-old woman presented with intermenstrual bleeding in the last 3 months (see report). Ultrasound: A 13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
OptD: Hysteroscopy and removal of the structure
highlight_terms_source: 13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium
why_right: An echogenic intracavitary structure in a woman with intermenstrual bleeding is an endometrial polyp. It is both symptomatic and 13 mm (over 1 cm), so the management is hysteroscopic polypectomy. Hysteroscopic removal treats the bleeding and gives the whole lesion for histology in one step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blind endometrial sampling can miss a focal polyp and does not remove it; sampling is the step for AUB over 45 or thickened endometrium without a focal lesion.
B. Repeat scanning (observation) is only for polyps that are asymptomatic AND under 1 cm; this one is symptomatic and 13 mm.
C. Progestogens do not remove a structural lesion; they are used for anovulatory bleeding or hyperplasia without atypia, not for a polyp.
key_concept:
Endometrial polyp: TVUS first, hysteroscopy confirms and treats.
  • Presents with menorrhagia or intermenstrual bleeding
  • Asymptomatic AND under 1 cm: observe
  • Symptomatic OR over 1 cm: hysteroscopic polypectomy
  • Removal gives histology (excludes hyperplasia or cancer)
exam_pearl: Symptoms OR size over 1 cm alone is enough to remove; only small AND silent polyps are watched.

stem: A woman in her 30s with heavy menstrual bleeding, she had 13mm?? polyp, and hemoglobin of 7 g/dL. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Heavy menstrual bleeding with a 13 mm polyp means a symptomatic polyp larger than 1 cm, and the treatment of a symptomatic or large endometrial polyp is hysteroscopic polypectomy. It removes the cause of the bleeding, gives tissue for histology, and preserves the uterus in a woman in her 30s. The Hb of 7 is managed alongside (iron, or transfusion if she is symptomatic or unstable), while removal of the polyp is the definitive management the recall keys.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hysterectomy is far too radical for a benign polyp in a young woman; it is kept for failed conservative treatment, completed family with other pathology, or malignancy.
C. Blood transfusion treats the consequence, not the cause. It becomes the first step when the anemia is symptomatic (fatigue, dizziness, tachycardia, hypotension) or bleeding is ongoing and heavy, which the stem does not describe; the source also highlighted this option.
key_concept:
Endometrial polyp: TVUS to detect, hysteroscopy to confirm and treat.
  • Presents with heavy or intermenstrual bleeding
  • Initial imaging: transvaginal ultrasound
  • Small (<1 cm) and asymptomatic: observe
  • Symptomatic or >1 cm: hysteroscopic polypectomy
  • Symptomatic or unstable anemia: transfuse first, then treat the cause
exam_pearl: If the stem says she is dizzy, tachycardic or hypotensive with this Hb, transfusion comes first.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Screenshot (numbered 41 in its source file) embedded under 633. Option A is bold with 'removal' red-highlighted; 'transfusion' in option C is also red-highlighted.
Other marked answers: Screenshot red highlight also on: C. Blood transfusion

stem: 62-year-old patient presented with vaginal bleeding. Investigations revealed a malignant tumor of uterine fundus. Which of the following groups of lymph nodes is likely affected in this condition and to be dissected during surgery?
why_right: A 62-year-old with vaginal bleeding and a malignant tumor of the uterine fundus has endometrial cancer. Lymph from the fundus follows the ovarian vessels in the infundibulopelvic ligament up to the para-aortic nodes, so these are at risk and are sampled or dissected during surgical staging.
why_wrong_block:
A. Superficial inguinal nodes drain the vulva, lower vagina and the uterine cornu along the round ligament; they are not the main drainage of the fundus.
B. Deep inguinal nodes receive lymph from the superficial inguinal nodes and the lower limb; they are not a staging group for uterine cancer.
C. Internal iliac nodes drain the cervix and lower uterine body; they would be the answer for a cervical or lower uterine tumor, not a fundal one.
key_concept:
Pelvic organ lymph follows the arterial supply.
  • Uterine fundus and ovary: para-aortic (via ovarian vessels)
  • Uterine cornu: superficial inguinal (via round ligament)
  • Cervix and lower uterus: internal and external iliac, obturator
  • Vulva and lower vagina: superficial inguinal
  • Endometrial cancer: biopsy to diagnose, surgical staging with pelvic and para-aortic nodes
exam_pearl: Fundus or ovary = para-aortic; cervix = iliac; vulva = inguinal.

stem: A 30-year-old woman P1+0 presented to Obstetrics and Gynecology Clinic complains of inability to conceive for the last 3 years. During that time, she was not on contraceptive and her menstrual periods every 45 days but no period for the last 6 months (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? TSH 9.2 U/L (0.4 - 5.0); FSH 5.3 U/L; LH 7.2 U/L; Prolactin 140 ng/ml (< 25 ng/ml)
why_right: The labs show a high TSH 9.2 with a raised prolactin 140 and normal FSH and LH. Primary hypothyroidism raises TRH, which stimulates prolactin release, and the hyperprolactinemia suppresses ovulation, giving oligomenorrhea, then amenorrhea and infertility. The single diagnosis that explains both abnormal results is hypothyroidism.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hypopituitarism lowers pituitary output (TSH, FSH, LH, prolactin); here TSH and prolactin are high.
C. Hyperprolactinemia is present but is secondary; a primary prolactinoma would not raise TSH, so always check TSH before blaming the pituitary.
D. PCOS needs hyperandrogenism or polycystic ovaries and often a raised LH:FSH ratio; none is given and it does not raise TSH.
key_concept:
High prolactin: check pregnancy and TSH before imaging the pituitary.
  • High TSH + high prolactin = primary hypothyroidism (TRH drives prolactin)
  • Normal TSH + very high prolactin = consider prolactinoma, drugs
  • Low FSH/LH/TSH together = hypopituitarism
  • High FSH = ovarian failure
  • PCOS: 2 of 3 (oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries); a raised LH:FSH ratio is supportive only
  • Treat with levothyroxine: prolactin and cycles normalise
exam_pearl: Raised prolactin with raised TSH is hypothyroidism, not a prolactinoma.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is complaining of vaginal discharge and burning with urination. Her husband was recently diagnosed with gonorrhea. Which of the following tests has the highest diagnostic value?
why_right: Her husband has gonorrhea and she has discharge with dysuria, so the question is where Neisseria gonorrhoeae lives in a woman. Gonococci infect columnar epithelium of the endocervix, so an endocervical swab (NAAT or culture) gives the highest diagnostic yield.
why_wrong_block:
A. A routine urine culture does not grow gonococci; first void urine NAAT is acceptable but less sensitive than a genital swab in women.
B. Rectal or anogenital swabs are added when there is anal exposure or anorectal symptoms; they are not the primary site in this presentation.
D. The vagina is lined by squamous epithelium that gonococci do not infect; a high vaginal swab is for candida, bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas.
key_concept:
Sample the site the organism infects.
  • Gonorrhea / Chlamydia in women: endocervical swab (culture or NAAT); vulvovaginal NAAT swab is equivalent
  • Men: first void urine or urethral swab
  • Candida, BV, trichomonas: high vaginal swab
  • Anal or oral exposure: add rectal or pharyngeal swabs
exam_pearl: Cervicitis organisms (gonorrhea, chlamydia) = endocervical swab; vaginitis organisms = high vaginal swab.

stem: A 35-week pregnant woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows placenta previa covering the os completely. She was stabilized, and the bleeding stopped. What is the most appropriate management?
OptC: Wait until 37 weeks, then do cesarean section
highlight_terms_source: placenta previa covering the os completely
why_right: A complete previa at 35 weeks whose bleeding has stopped in a stabilized mother is managed expectantly (admission and observation), aiming for planned cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks. This avoids prematurity while timing delivery before labor starts. Delivery is by cesarean only because the placenta covers the os.
why_wrong_block:
A. Induction of labor means vaginal delivery, which is contraindicated when the placenta covers the internal os.
B. Immediate cesarean is right for severe active bleeding, maternal instability or fetal distress before 37 weeks; here bleeding has stopped and she is stable.
D. Awaiting labor is unsafe and vaginal birth is impossible with a complete previa; delivery must be a planned cesarean before labor.
key_concept:
Placenta previa: cesarean only; timing depends on bleeding and gestation.
  • No vaginal exam until ultrasound localizes the placenta
  • Severe bleeding, unstable mother or fetal distress: stabilize and cesarean now
  • Mild or stopped bleeding before term: admit, steroids if <34 wk, MgSO4 if <32 wk
  • Then planned cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks
  • At term with bleeding: cesarean
exam_pearl: Bleeding stopped and stable = wait; active heavy bleeding or fetal distress = cut now.

stem: A woman planning for conception presented to the clinic concerned about vitamin D deficiency. She is dark skinned and vegetarian, and does not get adequate exposure to sunlight. What is the recommended daily dose of vitamin D?
highlight_terms_source: does not get adequate exposure to sunlight
why_right: She has several risk factors for deficiency: dark skin, a vegetarian diet and little sunlight. Women at high risk of vitamin D deficiency who are planning or in pregnancy are advised a higher prophylactic dose of about 1000 IU daily, rather than the routine dose given to low-risk women.
why_wrong_block:
A. 600 IU is the general recommended daily allowance for adults and pregnant women without risk factors; it is not enough for this high-risk woman.
C. 2000 IU is a higher dose used in some regimens for those with documented low levels; it is not the standard prophylactic dose for risk factors alone.
D. 4000 IU is the usual tolerable upper intake for adults, a ceiling, not a routine daily recommendation.
key_concept:
Vitamin D dose depends on risk.
  • Low-risk adult or pregnant woman: about 400 to 600 IU daily
  • High risk (dark skin, covered or indoors, vegetarian, obese): about 1000 IU daily
  • Confirmed deficiency: treatment doses, then maintenance
  • 4000 IU: upper limit, not a target
  • Pair with folic acid 0.4 mg preconception
exam_pearl: Risk factors listed (dark skin, low sun, vegetarian) push the answer above the routine dose to 1000 IU.

stem: A 19 years old primigravida complaining of abdominal cramps and vaginal spotting. LMP 6 weeks ago with a positive home pregnancy test. Speculum examination closed os and abdominal pain with cervical manipulation. What's the appropriate next step?
OptD: Further deeper vaginal examination to rule out masses
why_right: A woman 6 weeks after her LMP with a positive pregnancy test, cramps and spotting, a closed os and pain on cervical manipulation could have a threatened miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy. After history and speculum examination, the next step is transvaginal ultrasound to show whether the pregnancy is intrauterine and viable, and to look for an adnexal mass or free fluid.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC is supportive (anemia, blood loss) but cannot locate the pregnancy or decide the diagnosis.
C. CT exposes the fetus to radiation and is inferior to ultrasound for early pregnancy; it has no role here.
D. Further deep vaginal examination adds pain and, with a possible ectopic, risks rupture; imaging, not repeated palpation, is needed to rule out masses.
key_concept:
First-trimester bleeding: history and exam, then TVUS, then treat by type.
  • Closed os + viable intrauterine pregnancy: threatened miscarriage
  • Open os, products retained: inevitable or incomplete
  • Closed os, nonviable pregnancy on scan, often few symptoms: missed
  • Empty uterus + positive hCG: suspect ectopic, add serial beta-hCG
  • Cervical motion tenderness: think ectopic
exam_pearl: Cervical motion tenderness in early pregnancy means ectopic until TVUS proves otherwise.

stem: A 20-year-old primigravida in her first trimester is a heavy smoker. You advise her about the risks of smoking during pregnancy, but she refuses to quit. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptC: Join her to a smoking cessation support group
why_right: She is a 20-year-old adult who has been counselled and refuses to quit. In pregnancy, behavioural support is the first-line cessation intervention, and offering referral to a cessation support group keeps her engaged and builds motivation without coercion or breaching confidentiality.
why_wrong_block:
A. Informing her father breaches the confidentiality of a competent adult; family can be involved only with her consent.
B. Informing her mother is the same breach of confidentiality; her age makes her the decision maker.
D. NRT in pregnancy is considered only when she wants to quit and behavioural support alone has failed; drugs are pointless for someone not ready to stop.
key_concept:
Smoking in pregnancy: advise, support, then medicate if needed.
  • Risks: low birth weight and IUGR, miscarriage, preterm birth, abruption, stillbirth, SIDS
  • First line in pregnancy: counselling and behavioural support
  • Not ready to quit: motivational support, keep the door open
  • NRT: if behavioural support fails and she wants to quit
  • Varenicline and bupropion: generally avoided in pregnancy
  • Outside pregnancy: varenicline or combination NRT first line, bupropion an alternative
exam_pearl: An adult patient's refusal never justifies calling her parents; offer support and keep counselling.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): 'She has not thought about quitting.' Same options; C. Join her to a smoking cessation support group highlighted.

stem: A 32-year-old patient became pregnant through in-vitro fertilization. She is now 7 weeks pregnant and is scheduled for laparoscopic surgical excision of an ectopic pregnancy (see report). Ultrasound: Presence of a right-sided 4-cm ectopic pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate procedure?
OptC: Excision of both right and left tubes
why_right: This recall's key is right-sided salpingotomy alone: the aim is to remove the right ectopic while conserving tubal tissue in an IVF patient who wants a future pregnancy. Surgery itself is correct because a 4 cm mass fails the methotrexate size criterion (<4 cm). Note that the same scenario with a left hydrosalpinx on the report is keyed elsewhere to excision of both tubes; see the concern below.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hysterectomy is never the procedure for a tubal ectopic in a woman seeking fertility; it is reserved for uncontrollable uterine haemorrhage (e.g. cornual or scar rupture) when nothing else works.
C. Removing both tubes is justified only when the report shows a left hydrosalpinx, because hydrosalpinx fluid refluxes into the uterus and lowers IVF implantation; the recall's key chose tubal conservation instead.
D. Methotrexate needs a stable patient, hCG ≤5000, no cardiac activity and a mass <4 cm; a 4 cm ectopic fails the size rule, and an intraoperative injection is not a substitute for removing it.
key_concept:
Ectopic ≥4 cm or unstable: surgery; small, stable, criteria met: methotrexate.
  • MTX criteria: stable, hCG ≤5000, no fetal heart, mass <4 cm, reliable follow-up
  • Salpingectomy: usual surgical choice when the other tube is healthy
  • Salpingotomy: considered to preserve fertility, needs hCG follow-up for persistent trophoblast
  • IVF patient + hydrosalpinx: remove the hydrosalpinx to improve implantation
exam_pearl: Read the report: a left hydrosalpinx in an IVF patient flips the answer to excising both tubes.

stem: A 30-year-old primigravida presents to the Emergency Room complaining of vaginal spotting for the last few days, her history reveals irregularity of the menstrual cycles and that she has been trying to conceive for the last 3 years. Abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the lower abdomen and the pelvic examination reveals a closed cervical Os with cervical motion tenderness (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 105/min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Weight 60 kg, Height 160 cm. Hb 130 g/L; HCT 0.38; MCH 19; MCHC 330; MCV 85; Platelets 155; WBC 4.6. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptA: Perform an abdominal ultrasound of the pelvis
OptC: Know about the reason of infertility
why_right: A woman of reproductive age with spotting, irregular cycles, lower abdominal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness and a heart rate of 105 could have an ectopic pregnancy. Before any imaging or treatment, the first step is to confirm whether she is pregnant with a β-hCG; the result then directs the ultrasound and management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound comes after β-hCG, which tells you what to look for (and transvaginal, not abdominal, is preferred in early pregnancy); it would be first only once pregnancy is already confirmed.
C. The cause of her 3 year infertility is an elective outpatient work-up; it is irrelevant until an acute ectopic or other emergency is excluded.
D. Analgesia treats the symptom, not the cause; it is supportive and would never replace establishing pregnancy status first.
key_concept:
Any woman of reproductive age with pelvic pain or bleeding: β-hCG first.
  • β-hCG positive → transvaginal ultrasound for location
  • No intrauterine sac with hCG above the discriminatory level → suspect ectopic
  • Unstable + positive hCG → surgery after resuscitation
  • CMT also fits PID, which is considered once pregnancy is excluded
exam_pearl: Infertility history and IVF are ectopic risk factors; they raise, not lower, the need to check hCG first.

stem: A primigravida at 38 weeks gestation presented with irregular contractions. Upon assessment she had 4 cm cervical dilation, -2 station, intact membranes, and normal CTG. Three hours later there was no change and she was still having mild irregular contractions. What is the appropriate management?
OptC: Ask her to come later when she is in active labor
why_right: She has mild irregular contractions, 4 cm with -2 station, intact membranes and a normal CTG, and no change after 3 hours. That is the latent phase (or prodromal labor), not active labor, and the latent phase can normally last many hours. With mother and fetus well, there is nothing to correct, so she can be sent home and asked to return when contractions become regular and painful.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin augmentation is for the active phase when contractions are inadequate and the cervix has not changed for about 6 hours; it is not used to speed up a normal latent phase.
B. Amniotomy is an augmentation step in established labor; with the head high at -2 and no active labor, it risks cord prolapse and commits her to delivery without an indication.
key_concept:
Latent phase with reassuring mother and fetus: reassure and send home; augment only in the active phase.
  • Latent phase: up to 4 to <6 cm; may last up to about 20 h in a nullipara
  • Active phase: >4 to 6 cm with regular contractions
  • Active phase, adequate contractions, no change 4 h → C-section
  • Active phase, inadequate contractions, no change 6 h → oxytocin, then C-section if it fails
  • Ruptured membranes at term not in labor → induction
exam_pearl: Prolonged latent phase is not a labor arrest; arrest rules apply only once she is in the active phase.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Women in labor 1 cm dilated with irregular contraction evaluated for 3 hours with no progression. A. Amniotomy, B. Send her home and come back if ready (not by word but something like that) [highlighted], C. Induction of labor.

stem: A female pregnant at 23 weeks gestation came to antenatal clinic all previous pregnancy uncomplicated, her mother have T2DM and she is asking about GDM screening?
OptB: Random blood sugar at this visit
OptC: 75g oral glucose tolerance test at 28-32 weeks
why_right: She is 23 weeks, has a first-degree relative with T2DM and no previous GDM, so she needs routine GDM testing in the usual third-trimester window rather than anything today. The one-step diagnostic test is the 75 g, 2-hour OGTT, which is what this option offers.
why_wrong_block:
A. HbA1c is not used to diagnose GDM; it is used to detect pre-existing diabetes early in pregnancy or to judge control in known diabetics.
B. A random glucose is neither a screening nor a diagnostic test for GDM in an asymptomatic woman; it would only matter if she had symptoms of overt hyperglycaemia.
D. The 3-hour 100 g test is the second (diagnostic) step of the two-step approach, done only after an abnormal 1-hour 50 g challenge; it is not the first test offered.
key_concept:
GDM testing: 24 to 28 weeks; early testing if previous GDM.
  • One-step: 2-hour 75 g OGTT
  • Two-step: 1-hour 50 g challenge → if positive, 3-hour 100 g OGTT
  • HbA1c: not diagnostic for GDM
  • Diagnosed GDM: diet and exercise first, insulin if targets not met
exam_pearl: The standard window is 24 to 28 weeks; the 28 to 32 in the option is likely how it was recalled, so pick by the test type (75 g OGTT).

stem: 60 female has post menopausal bleeding for 8 months what confirm diagnosis
why_right: A 60-year-old with post-menopausal bleeding for 8 months has endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Only tissue confirms the diagnosis, and that tissue comes from the endometrium, so endometrial biopsy is the confirmatory test (AUB over 45 → endometrial sampling).
why_wrong_block:
A. Cervical biopsy is for a visible cervical lesion or an abnormal Pap/colposcopy (postcoital bleeding points to the cervix); it does not sample the endometrium.
C. A vaginal (speculum) exam is part of the initial assessment to find the bleeding source, but it gives no tissue and cannot confirm a diagnosis.
key_concept:
Endometrial sampling rules:
  • AUB at age >45 → endometrial biopsy
  • Post-menopausal bleeding + endometrial thickness >5 mm → biopsy
  • Asymptomatic post-menopausal + thickness ≥11 mm → biopsy
  • <45 with unopposed estrogen (PCOS, obesity) or failed medical therapy → biopsy
  • MRI and CA-125 are not diagnostic; MRI is for staging
exam_pearl: "Confirm diagnosis" = tissue; ultrasound triages but never confirms endometrial cancer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same question shown twice. Numbered 727: '70 or 80 female has post menopausal bleeding for 8 months. I dont remember if next step or most appropriate or highest diagnostic?' A. cervical biopsy / B. endometrial biopsy (highlighted). The 'Q:' version adds C. Vaginal exam and also highlights endometrial biopsy.

stem: 22 years old female coming for annual care. She is has no complaint, married for 2 years, on OCP, have depression on fluoxetine, no family history of cancer or cardiac disease. What screening should be done at this time?
why_right: She is 22, asymptomatic, and here for annual care. Cervical cancer screening starts at 21, with Pap cytology every 3 years from 21 to 29, so a Pap smear is the screening due now. Her OCP use, fluoxetine and negative family history do not change this.
why_wrong_block:
B. Mammography is not a screening test at 22 in an average-risk woman; routine screening starts at 40, earlier only with high genetic or family risk.
C. The option text was not recalled; whatever it was, Pap cytology is the screening test indicated at this age.
D. Pelvic ultrasound is not a screening test in asymptomatic women; it is used to investigate symptoms or an abnormal exam.
key_concept:
Cervical screening schedule:
  • Starts at 21, regardless of sexual history
  • 21 to 29: Pap cytology every 3 years
  • 30 to 65: co-test every 5 years or Pap alone every 3 years
  • >65 with adequate negative screening: stop
exam_pearl: Age, not marriage or sexual activity, starts cervical screening.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): female recently married, she is 23-24 (anyway more than 21), otherwise normal, what is screening or health promotion now: A. Pap smear [highlighted], B. Mammo.

stem: A 20-year-old divorced woman came for a Pap test. When is it recommended?
why_right: She is 20. Cervical screening begins at 21 regardless of sexual history, marriage or divorce, so a screening Pap is not recommended now but is due in about one year when she turns 21.
why_wrong_block:
A. Screening under 21 is not recommended even if sexually active, because cervical changes at this age usually regress and treatment causes harm; she would be screened now only if she were already 21 or older.
C. Three years is the repeat interval after a normal Pap between 21 and 29, not the time to the first screen.
D. Symptoms (postcoital bleeding, discharge) call for a diagnostic exam at any age; screening does not wait for symptoms.
key_concept:
First Pap at 21, then every 3 years until 29.
  • <21: no screening, whatever the sexual history
  • 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years
  • 30 to 65: co-test every 5 years or cytology every 3 years
exam_pearl: At 20 the answer is "wait until 21", which this recall phrases as "after 1 year".

stem: A 30-year-old married, nulligravid woman with symptomatic multiple uterine fibroids, all subserosal, underwent myomectomy. According to her operative note, the endometrial cavity was entered during surgery. What is the risk of placenta accreta during future pregnancies?
why_right: This recall's key is "Not affected", presumably reasoning that the fibroids were "all subserosal" and the patient is "nulligravid" with no cesarean scar. However, the stem stresses that the "endometrial cavity was entered", and standard teaching holds that any uterine surgery breaching the endometrium damages the endometrial and myometrial interface and raises placenta accreta risk. Learn the key, but be ready for exams keyed to "Increase".
why_wrong_block:
A. Increase is the answer most standard sources favour, because cavity entry at myomectomy leaves an endometrial scar like a cesarean; it is not the key on this recall.
B. Decrease is never correct: uterine scarring can only raise accreta risk or leave it unchanged.
C. Unknown is wrong because the association between prior uterine surgery and accreta is well established.
key_concept:
Placenta accreta spectrum: placenta invades because the decidua is deficient at a scar.
  • Strongest risk: previous cesarean section(s), especially with placenta previa
  • Other scars: myomectomy entering the cavity, curettage, Asherman syndrome
  • Subserosal myomectomy without cavity entry: little effect on the endometrium
  • Accreta (attached to myometrium), increta (into myometrium), percreta (through serosa)
exam_pearl: The clue "endometrial cavity was entered" is what makes the standard answer Increase; the key here says Not affected.

stem: A 39-year-old G8 P5126 at 38 weeks' gestation presents for induction of labor due to decreased fetal movement. She is started on oxytocin and begins having contractions. After several hours of labor, her cervix dilates to 6 cm, but she then develops a fever and fetal tachycardia. A diagnosis of chorioamnionitis is entertained. She delivers a baby boy vaginally 4 hours later, but afterward, there is a large continuous vaginal bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
why_right: Large continuous bleeding after delivery is PPH, and atony is the commonest cause. This woman also stacks atony risk factors: grand multiparity (G8), prolonged oxytocin exposure, and chorioamnionitis, all of which impair myometrial contraction.
why_wrong_block:
B. Placenta accreta presents with failure of placental separation and bleeding during attempted removal; usually linked to prior cesarean with previa, which is not described.
C. Cervical laceration follows instrumental or precipitous delivery and bleeds despite a firm uterus; nothing here suggests it.
D. Vaginal laceration likewise needs trauma clues (instrumental delivery, macrosomia, visible tear); none are given.
key_concept:
Uterine atony risk factors:
  • Overdistension: twins, polyhydramnios, macrosomia
  • Grand multiparity
  • Prolonged or augmented labor, prolonged oxytocin
  • Chorioamnionitis
  • Tocolytics (MgSO4) or general anesthesia
exam_pearl: Oxytocin exposure + chorioamnionitis + grand multipara = atony.

stem: A 30-year-old woman had a spontaneous vaginal delivery for a term twin pregnancy 2 hours ago. Now she has active vaginal bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
why_right: Active bleeding 2 hours after delivery is primary PPH, and atony is the commonest cause. A twin pregnancy overdistends the uterus, which then contracts poorly after delivery, making atony even more likely.
why_wrong_block:
B. Coagulopathy is an uncommon cause and nothing (abruption, preeclampsia, DIC, bleeding history) suggests it.
C. Genital tract trauma is the second commonest cause; it needs clues such as instrumental delivery, a visible tear, or bleeding with a firm uterus.
D. Retained tissue is less common and no incomplete placenta is described.
key_concept:
PPH is atony until proven otherwise.
  • Primary PPH: within 24 hours of delivery
  • Secondary PPH: 24 hours to 12 weeks
  • Overdistension (twins, polyhydramnios, macrosomia) predisposes to atony
  • First step: check tone, massage, oxytocin
exam_pearl: Twins = overdistended uterus = atony.

stem: A 38-year-old woman, known for low-lying placenta, delivered a normal vaginal delivery. One hour post-delivery, she had postpartum hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: PPH one hour after a normal vaginal delivery is most likely due to uterine atony, the commonest cause of PPH. The low-lying placenta does not change this; if anything, the placenta implanted on the poorly contractile lower segment makes placental-bed bleeding more likely.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulopathy is uncommon and nothing in the stem suggests a clotting problem.
C. Uterine inversion is rare, occurs at placental delivery (often with cord traction on a fundal placenta), and presents with shock, a vaginal mass and an absent fundus.
D. Genital tract trauma is the second commonest cause; no instrumental delivery, laceration or firm uterus is described.
key_concept:
PPH cause by clue:
  • No specific clue: atony
  • Firm uterus or visible tear: trauma
  • Mass in vagina, absent fundus, shock: inversion
  • Oozing from all sites, DIC trigger: coagulopathy
  • Low-lying placenta: lower segment contracts poorly, still atony/placental bed
exam_pearl: Do not let 'low-lying placenta' distract you: atony remains the answer.

stem: A 24-year-old woman just delivered her first baby with a birth weight of 2.7 kg while she was at 38 weeks of gestation. She is not known to have any medical or surgical history. She has a heavy gush of bleeding postpartum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: not known to have any medical or surgical history
why_right: A "heavy gush of bleeding postpartum" is postpartum hemorrhage, and uterine atony is by far its most common cause. With no history pointing to a bleeding disorder, no traumatic or instrumental delivery, and no incomplete placenta described, the default answer is atony: PPH is atony until proven otherwise.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cervical injury is the next most common cause, suspected when bleeding continues despite a FIRM, well contracted uterus or after instrumental or precipitous delivery; none of that is described here.
C. Coagulation defects would be suspected with a known bleeding disorder, abruption, severe preeclampsia/HELLP, sepsis or massive transfusion; she has no medical history.
D. Retained placental fragments are suspected when the placenta is incomplete on inspection or bleeding is delayed/secondary; no incomplete placenta is mentioned.
key_concept:
PPH causes, the 4 Ts (most to least common):
  • Tone: atony, soft boggy uterus, most common
  • Trauma: cervical/vaginal laceration, uterus firm
  • Tissue: retained placenta or fragments, incomplete placenta
  • Thrombin: coagulopathy
  • First step: check uterine tone, then massage and uterotonics
exam_pearl: If the stem says the uterus is FIRM and contracted, atony is out; think genital tract laceration next.

stem: A 24-year-old woman primigravida undergoes an uneventful vaginal delivery at term. After placental delivery, she has 1000 cc of vaginal bleeding. She is alert, and her vital signs are stable, with the uterus noted to be firm. Which of the following is the most common cause?
why_right: Bleeding of 1000 mL after placental delivery is postpartum hemorrhage. The decisive clue is that the uterus is firm, meaning normal tone, so atony is excluded; with a well-contracted uterus the most common remaining cause is genital tract laceration (the second commonest cause of PPH overall).
why_wrong_block:
A. Atony is the commonest cause of PPH overall, but it gives a soft, boggy uterus; a firm uterus rules it out here.
B. Coagulopathy is uncommon and needs a trigger (abruption, preeclampsia, amniotic fluid embolism, known bleeding disorder); none follows an uneventful delivery.
D. Retained products typically stop the uterus contracting well (boggy uterus) or follow an incomplete placenta; neither is described.
key_concept:
PPH: check uterine tone first (the 4 Ts).
  • Tone (atony): soft, boggy uterus; commonest cause
  • Trauma: bleeding with a FIRM uterus; second commonest
  • Tissue: retained placenta or fragments
  • Thrombin: coagulopathy
exam_pearl: PPH + firm uterus = look for a laceration; boggy uterus = atony.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is seen post-delivery with postpartum hemorrhage. She had a forceps delivery of a 3.7 kg baby. Examination revealed laceration of the cervix, vagina, and the perineal body. Which of the following is the most likely cause of postpartum hemorrhage?
highlight_terms_source: laceration of the cervix, vagina, and the perineal body
why_right: The examination itself shows the bleeding source: "laceration of the cervix, vagina, and the perineal body". A forceps delivery of a large (3.7 kg) baby is a classic risk factor for genital tract trauma, so the PPH here is from Trauma, one of the 4 Ts.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulopathy (Thrombin) is suggested by oozing from many sites, abruption, preeclampsia or DIC; here there is a visible anatomic source.
B. Uterine inversion presents at placental delivery with shock, a mass in the vagina and an absent fundus on abdominal palpation; none is described.
D. Retained placental tissue (Tissue) gives an incomplete placenta and a uterus that fails to stay contracted; it would not explain visible lacerations.
key_concept:
PPH causes, the 4 Ts: Tone > Trauma > Tissue > Thrombin.
  • Tone (atony): soft, boggy uterus; most common overall
  • Trauma: bleeding with a FIRM uterus, or lacerations seen; risk with instrumental delivery, big baby
  • Tissue: incomplete placenta, uterus not contracting well
  • Thrombin: abruption, preeclampsia, DIC, known bleeding disorder
exam_pearl: Atony is the commonest cause of PPH, but once lacerations are seen on exam (or the uterus is firm) the answer is trauma.

stem: Woman had normal vaginal delivery 12 days ago, now she present with postpartum hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely cause ?
why_right: Bleeding 12 days after delivery is secondary PPH (after 24 hours up to 12 weeks). The usual cause of late bleeding is retained products of conception, often with superimposed endometritis, which prevents the placental site from involuting.
why_wrong_block: A. Uterine atony is the most common cause of primary PPH (within 24 hours, soft boggy uterus); it is not the typical cause of bleeding nearly two weeks later.
key_concept:
Timing decides the cause of PPH.
  • Primary (<24 h): atony most common, then genital tract trauma, retained tissue, coagulopathy
  • Firm uterus with primary PPH → think laceration
  • Secondary (24 h to 12 weeks): retained products and/or endometritis
  • Secondary PPH work-up: ultrasound for retained tissue, treat infection
exam_pearl: "Most common cause of PPH" with no timing = atony; days to weeks after delivery = retained products.

stem: Asymptomatic Pregnant lady with urine culture positive for E coli but negative nitrate. What is the appropriate action?
highlight_terms_source: urine culture positive for E coli
why_right: A positive urine culture for E. coli in an asymptomatic pregnant woman is asymptomatic bacteriuria, which must be treated in pregnancy to prevent pyelonephritis and its obstetric complications. Culture is the reference test, so a negative nitrite on dipstick does not cancel a positive culture.
why_wrong_block:
B. Urinalysis is less sensitive than culture (nitrite can be negative with a short bladder dwell time); repeating it adds nothing once the culture is positive.
C. Waiting for symptoms is the approach for non-pregnant women; in pregnancy untreated bacteriuria can progress to pyelonephritis, so treat now.
key_concept:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat only in pregnancy (or before urological procedures, in renal transplant).
  • Screen with urine culture at the first antenatal visit
  • Nitrofurantoin: first line, avoid in the 3rd trimester
  • 3rd trimester: amoxicillin is a safe option
  • Fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides: avoid in pregnancy
  • Postpartum or non-pregnant: no treatment
exam_pearl: Pregnant + asymptomatic + positive culture = antibiotics; the dipstick result is a distractor.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variants in same block, all highlighting antibiotics: 'Pregnant lady in 13 weeks gestation with urine culture positive for E coli 100.000 positive Nitrate, asymptomatic' (antibiotics); 'Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy?' (treat with antibiotics vs just reassure); 'Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy screening 12 weeks, what to do?' (Give Abx vs Give Abx if symptomatic -> Give Abx).

stem: Postpartum woman found to have asymptomatic bacteriuria after delivery. Most appropriate management?
why_right: After delivery she is no longer pregnant, and she is asymptomatic. Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a non-pregnant woman without a special indication (renal transplant, urological procedure) is not treated, so no treatment is needed. Other alternatives a student might consider, such as oral antibiotics, are wrong for the same reason.
why_wrong_block: A. IV antibiotics are for pyelonephritis or sepsis (fever, flank pain, rigors); with no symptoms there is no infection to treat, and treating bacteriuria here only drives resistance.
key_concept:
Who gets treated for asymptomatic bacteriuria:
  • Pregnant: yes
  • Before a urological procedure with mucosal bleeding: yes
  • Renal transplant: yes
  • Postpartum, elderly, diabetic, catheterised: no
exam_pearl: The same culture is treated during pregnancy and ignored after delivery; the pregnancy status flips the answer.

stem: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks of gestation is found to have a cervical length of 27 mm on transvaginal ultrasound. What is the next step in management?
why_right: The decisive number is the cervical length: 27 mm is above the 25 mm cut off, so this cervix is not short. With no history of previous second trimester loss or preterm birth given, a cervical length >25 mm means routine antenatal care, which is expectant management. Nothing here (no contractions, no bleeding, no membrane change) calls for an intervention.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cerclage is for a woman with a previous second trimester loss whose cervix measures <25 mm before 24 weeks (or history indicated at 13 to 14 weeks); here the cervix is 27 mm and she is already at 24 weeks, beyond which cerclage is generally not recommended.
B. Vaginal progesterone is the screening pathway answer when the cervix is short (<25 mm) in a woman without a prior second trimester loss; 27 mm is above that threshold.
D. Tocolysis suppresses contractions in established preterm labor to buy time for steroids; she has no contractions, and tocolytics do not treat a cervix.
key_concept:
Cervical length 25 mm is the magic number (screened 16 to 24 weeks).
  • No prior 2nd trimester loss, CL >25 mm: routine care (expectant)
  • No prior loss, CL <25 mm: vaginal progesterone
  • Prior 2nd trimester loss: history indicated cerclage at 13 to 14 weeks
  • Prior loss on serial scans, CL <25 mm before 24 weeks: ultrasound indicated cerclage
  • Contractions with cervical change: preterm labor pathway (steroids, MgSO4, tocolysis)
exam_pearl: Read the number carefully: 27 mm is reassuring; the same stem with 20 mm flips the answer to progesterone (or cerclage if she had a prior loss).

stem: A 29-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room with a very heavy period. She is morbidly obese and diabetic. Her periods are irregular, occurring every 3-4 months. She had her period 2 weeks ago and it has not stopped, with heavy clots. Pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: periods are irregular, occurring every 3-4 months
why_right: "Morbidly obese and diabetic" (insulin resistance) with periods "every 3-4 months" describes chronic anovulation, PCOS type. Without ovulation there is no progesterone, so the endometrium builds up under unopposed estrogen and eventually sheds heavily and for a prolonged time, here 2 weeks with clots. This is AUB-O in the PALM-COEIN system; with obesity and long-standing anovulation, endometrial sampling should be considered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fibroids cause heavy but regular, cyclic menses; they do not explain cycles only every 3 to 4 months.
B. A bleeding disorder (e.g. von Willebrand) usually presents with heavy regular periods from menarche and other bleeding history; nothing here suggests it.
C. The pregnancy test is negative, which excludes any type of abortion.
key_concept:
Irregular infrequent cycles + heavy prolonged bleed = anovulatory AUB (AUB-O).
  • Risk clues: obesity, diabetes/insulin resistance, PCOS, extremes of reproductive age
  • Mechanism: unopposed estrogen, no progesterone withdrawal
  • Heavy but regular cycles: think fibroids or bleeding disorder
  • Always exclude pregnancy first
  • Long-standing anovulation + obesity: consider endometrial sampling
exam_pearl: Regular heavy cycles point to structural or coagulation causes; irregular infrequent cycles with heavy bleeds point to anovulation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman asking for effective and reversible method of contraceptive, which if the following is the most effective?
why_right: The question asks which option is most effective while reversible. The hormonal vaginal ring works like the combined pill (suppresses ovulation), with a typical-use failure rate of roughly 7 per 100 women per year. All the other options are barrier or chemical methods that depend on correct use at every act, so they fail more often.
why_wrong_block:
B. The female condom has a typical-use failure rate of about 21 per 100 women per year, much higher than the ring; it is chosen when woman-controlled STI protection is the priority.
C. The male condom fails in about 13 per 100 women per year with typical use; it is the right answer when the question asks about protection against STIs, not maximum pregnancy prevention.
D. Spermicide alone is among the least effective methods (about 21 per 100 per year with typical use); it is mainly used as an adjunct to barrier methods.
key_concept:
Typical-use failure rates (per 100 women per year) rank hormonal methods above barrier methods.
  • Vaginal ring about 7
  • Male condom about 13
  • Female condom about 21
  • Spermicide about 21
  • LARC (IUD, implant) under 1, beating all of these if offered
exam_pearl: If an IUD or implant appears in the options, it beats the ring; and if the question asks about STI prevention, the condom wins.
